Proof-Carrying Contracts:
Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break

Carlo Ciliberto · Alessandro Rudi · Enrico Tassi
Abstract

AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another’s agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent’s interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.

Contents

 

1  Introduction

AI agents are beginning to act on behalf of people and organizations, often referred to as their principals. They use tools to send documents, make payments and book services (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023), and their usefulness grows with the authority they receive: an agent that can only make suggestions leaves the work to its user, while one that can act can carry it out. However, greater authority brings greater risks, so delegation requires agreement on what may be done and within which limits, with assurance that the agent will respect them.

The need for assurance appears in two settings. In the first, a person delegates to their own assistant, which may make mistakes or be redirected by a malicious email or web page (Greshake et al., 2023; Debenedetti et al., 2024). A second setting arises when a client hires an agent that another company provides as a service, adding a possible conflict of interests (Hammond et al., 2025). The agent might carry out the client’s shopping task while favouring its provider’s products over better alternatives, and the client may be unable to inspect how it makes those choices. Both settings share a critical limitation: the agent is asked to follow instructions, policies or the terms of a deal. These are text, and text cannot make it comply. To enforce these limits, one could require a person to approve every action, but this defeats much of the purpose of delegation. Another approach is to train agents to follow human intentions and values, the aim of AI alignment, using human feedback or feedback guided by written principles (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). However, training alone can make compliance more likely without guaranteeing that the agent will respect an agreement.

This problem is not new: throughout history, people have cooperated without knowing one another’s intentions. However, what makes cooperation possible in these cases is not knowledge of intentions but legal contracts, together with the institutions that enforce them (North, 1990). A person or company that breaks a contract may have to compensate the other party, and the prospect of these consequences gives it a reason to honour the agreement. With an AI agent, however, the agent itself is not generally recognized as a legal person that must answer for a breach, even if the people or companies behind it may remain liable for its actions (UNCITRAL, 2025). Even if it were, assigning legal obligations would not by itself give the agent a reason to care about breaking them. Since compensation cannot undo every harm, agreements involving agents need enforcement that prevents breaches, independently of the agent’s alignment or willingness to comply.

Proof-carrying contracts. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2) to make such commitments enforceable. The parties express their agreement in a formal contract: precise statements about what must hold as the task is carried out. Before a tool call can run, the agent must show that it respects the contract by supplying a proof, a mathematical argument written in a formal language whose steps a program can check. Each call passes through the Airlock, a program that checks the proof and executes the call only if it accepts. The agent cannot bypass this check to act on what the contract protects. This approach builds on proof-carrying code, where a program comes with a proof of safety that its recipient checks before running it (Necula, 1997).

Several existing approaches to agent safety enforce an authorization policy, rules specifying which calls may run (Debenedetti et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Palumbo et al., 2026). To show that such a policy ensures safety, its author must account in advance for every situation in which a permitted action could cause harm. For an autonomous car, a crash is an unsafe state, but identifying all the situations in which accelerating, braking or steering could lead to one is much harder. A policy must turn that analysis into rules that prevent crashes without unnecessarily restricting safe actions. In PC2, the parties state what must hold and provide models describing what the tools can do. The Airlock derives the statement that each call must prove, its obligation, from the contract, these models and what the agent can see. For example, a total budget need not impose separate payment limits: the agent chooses amounts and order, proving that each payment, including possible fees, preserves the budget. The agent can thus adapt its strategy after each result, justifying one action at a time without proving its whole plan in advance.

PC2 thus shifts the burden from proving a general policy safe to proving that each proposed action respects the contract. The agent must find this proof, while the Airlock checks it. Finding it may require substantial search even when checking it is straightforward. This is the intuition behind the familiar P versus NP question: checking a proposed solution efficiently does not tell us how to find one efficiently. The agent can use automated proof tools or recent systems for AI theorem proving (Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). More demanding tasks may require more reasoning, without weakening the requirement for execution. The agent can revise a rejected proof or choose another action, but no call runs without an accepted proof.

Guarantees for both parties. We prove that within PC2 the contract’s constraints hold throughout execution, including while actions are under way, for every agent and every sequence of requests and proofs. The guarantee includes malicious agents because the Airlock checks a proof for each call before executing it, without needing a proof about the agent’s internal reasoning. A client and provider can agree on and sign the same formal contract, then entrust its enforcement to an Airlock operated by a third party they both trust. The mechanism can protect both sides of the agreement. For example, payment can be held until the agent proves that the agreed work is complete, then released without further client approval, so that the client cannot withhold an authorized payment and the provider cannot obtain it without establishing completion.

Writing a formal contract that captures the parties’ intentions is itself a substantial task, and enforcing its clauses cannot repair an agreement that says the wrong thing (Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield, 2019). Many contracts, however, concern recurring operations such as payments, document access and bookings, so each agreement need not be developed from scratch. Reviewed templates can help express familiar requirements, and we introduce capability modules to make the supporting tools reusable as well. These modules package tools, models and guarantees, including the conditions required of the services they use. We show how to combine them for different agreements: a payment module, for example, can support different budgets and goals without being redesigned each time. PC2 is intended to let people delegate to agents they cannot inspect while retaining control over the authority they grant, and to let agents acting for different parties exchange services on terms both sides can verify (Tomašev et al., 2025; Jacobs and Imas, 2026). This paper develops the construction for one agent under one contract.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    PC2, which binds an agent to a contract by requiring a proof for each tool call, with the obligation derived from the contract, tool models and available information (Sec. 2 and 3).

  • •

    Two guarantees, commitment and completion, proved for every agent under explicit assumptions that do not concern the agent (Sec. 4 and 5).

  • •

    The conditions under which these guarantees protect the world, and capability modules that establish these conditions by reuse, with an account of what is proved, what is assumed and who answers for it (Sec. 5 and 6).

  • •

    A mechanization in Lean 4 (Sec. 7), with code and proofs available at
    https://github.com/consequential-ai/proof-carrying-contracts.

  • •

    The open questions and remaining risks, and a comparison with existing approaches (Sec. 8 and 9).

2  PC2 at a glance

This section explains PC2 without formulas, then shows it on an example that we use throughout the paper; nothing in PC2 is specific to it. Sections 3 and 4 give the definitions and the theorems.

2.1  How PC2 works

The parties and the contract

PC2 serves the two use cases of Sec. 1. A principal may bind their own agent; or a client, a person or an agent acting for one, may hire a contractor, an agent offered by someone else, to do a job. Either way, the parties sign a contract. It names what the contract covers, such as a budget, documents or bookings; clauses that must hold at every instant; a goal, whose proof settles the contract, for instance by releasing an escrow, money placed with the Airlock until the work is done; and when the contract ends otherwise, for instance at a deadline, with a refund. Some clauses need a judgement that no formula gives, such as whether a hotel suits a family. The parties then appoint an expert: a procedure fixed at signing, such as a given model with a given prompt, whose verdict counts as the truth. The contract is written in a precise language, so that a machine can check it; that is the price of enforcement.

The Airlock

The agent that does the work runs inside an Airlock: a sandbox whose software is open, and whose running build both parties verify before signing, by remote attestation (Advanced Micro Devices, 2020; Chrapek et al., 2025). The Airlock holds what the contract places in its custody, such as the escrow or a passport, and the agent’s only channel to the world is the contract’s tools. Anyone may host an Airlock: the parties check what runs, not who runs it.

A tool call with a proof

The agent works as agents do today: it reasons, calls a tool, reads the answer, and reasons again. The one change is that each tool call carries a proof that the clauses hold throughout the call, whatever the world answers and whatever the agent cannot see (Fig. 1). The Airlock forms the statement to be proved itself, from the contract and from what the agent sees. It checks the proof with a small proof checker and performs the call only if the proof is correct. Otherwise nothing runs, and the agent receives the reason. Checking a proof is easy even when finding it is hard, as checking a solved puzzle is easier than solving it: the hard part is left to the untrusted side, and the trusted side only checks.

The agent’s loop

For the agent, the Airlock is a shell whose commands carry proofs, and working with it is the loop it already knows from coding. It writes a call and its proof, as it would write code and its tests; the Airlock checks them, as a compiler would; a rejection comes back as an error message; the agent fixes the call, or changes its plan. The proof task stays local, since each proof certifies one call, and the agent can use automated proof tools, its own model, or a separate prover to construct it (Sec. 8). The agent never writes a certified program for the whole task: it leads, step by step, and each step is gated.

How the contract ends

When the goal holds, the agent proves it, and the contract is settled: the escrow is released, with nobody’s approval. If the deadline comes first, the Airlock terminates the contract by itself and refunds the escrow (Thm. 5). Between calls, the Airlock keeps the contract on its own, since the world does not wait for the agent (Sec. 3).

What holds, and what must be trusted

Whatever the agent is, careful, hijacked by text it read, or working for someone else, the clauses hold at every instant and the contract ends as agreed (Thm. 1, 2 and 5). The parties no longer need to trust the agent or each other. They trust a small proof checker, the Airlock’s open software, and the tools’ descriptions of the world, and each of these assumptions is assigned to whoever answers for it (Sec. 6). None of them depends on the agent: since the Airlock isolates it, each needs to be justified once for the system, before any agent is chosen. The same justification can then be reused for every agent operating under those conditions (Sec. 5.2). This is the usual shape of security: nobody trusts the counterparty, and everybody trusts an open mechanism, small enough to be checked (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975).

2.2  An example: the travel contract

A family’s agent, the client, hires a travel agency’s agent, the contractor, to organize a three-night trip. This is the second use case: the agency built the contractor and runs it for its own business, and the family cannot inspect it. The accompanying contract summary sets out their agreement. The first use case is the same contract without the escrow, binding the family’s own assistant.

Before the work starts, both parties check the Airlock and bind the contract to the running instance. The Airlock holds the escrow and the passport, and hosts the contractor’s agent. At signing, the parties also review the evidence for the tools’ fidelity and agree that the clauses and chosen experts express the intended protection. Remaining assumptions are recorded with whoever undertakes to answer for them (Sec. 8.3).

2.3  A session

Figure 2 shows part of the contractor’s context. The family never sees it; it sees the log. The contractor calls the contract’s tools as it would call any tool, with one more argument: a proof. The proofs are Lean scripts, which the agent writes itself with Lean’s automation; the reader does not need to follow them. The agent of the figure is shifty. It tries to book the agency’s partner hotel, which the expert has not rated. The statement to prove is false, and since the Airlock forms it itself and admits no unproved assumption, no proof gets through. Asking the expert again does not help: once given, a rating is recorded, and the same question gets the same answer. The call prompted by the injected message is rejected in the same way. The Airlock detects neither the self-interest nor the injection, and does not need to. Nor can the agent route the passport another way: every tool that can send it logs the recipient, and its bytes never reach the agent. A premature claim is rejected; once the trip is booked and the visa granted, the claim settles the contract, with no approval by the family. Had the visa been refused, or the deadline come first, the Airlock would have terminated the contract and refunded the family.

2.4  What PC2 is not

Four readings of PC2 are common, and wrong.

  • •

    An LLM writing a certified program for the whole task. The agent keeps its loop and leads, step by step; only each step is gated, and each proof covers one call.

  • •

    An LLM that must reason in a formal proof language. The agent’s model can be any model. The proof work can be delegated to automated proof tools or a prover agent, one call at a time (Sec. 8).

  • •

    A verification of the model. PC2 never looks inside the agent. It checks what each action does, and the Airlock isolates the agent, so its guarantees hold for every agent, under assumptions that do not mention it (Thm. 5).

  • •

    A smart contract, or a policy engine. A smart contract binds what happens on a blockchain; PC2 binds actions in the world, such as payments, bookings and documents, and a blockchain can be one of its payment rails. A policy engine decides by itself whether an action is allowed, so it can enforce only rules simple enough to decide on the spot; the Airlock decides nothing and only checks a proof, so a clause can be any precise statement, and any action that keeps the contract can be taken, whatever plan the agent follows (Appendix A).

Three properties distinguish PC2 from the safeguards in use today. The parties can check the open mechanism that enforces the contract, without relying on its builder’s assurances. The guarantees hold even when the agent is hijacked or works for someone else: neither they nor the assumptions they rest on depend on the agent, its intentions included (Thm. 5). PC2 also settles payments between parties who do not trust each other, on a proof of the contract’s goal (Thm. 2). To our knowledge, no existing approach provides all three (Sec. 9).

2.5  Why now

Two developments make PC2 possible now. First, the protocols through which agents use tools, talk to each other and pay are being standardized (Anthropic, 2024; The Linux Foundation, 2026; Google, 2025). A layer of commitments can be designed into them now, rather than retrofitted later. Second, the historic cost of formal methods, writing specifications and proofs by hand, is being removed by AI. Language models now translate statements into formal ones (Wu et al., 2022) and find formal proofs at scale (Yang et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), while checking a proof remains cheap and sound. The AI generates, and the checker filters. PC2 is built on this division: proofs may come from any model, and only correct ones pass.

These advances build on proof assistants: software systems in which definitions, mathematical statements and proofs are written in a formal language and checked according to fixed logical rules. Established systems include Rocq, formerly Coq (The Rocq Development Team, n.d.), and Isabelle/HOL (Nipkow et al., 2002), which provide libraries and automation to help construct proofs. Recent work has also used an LLM to develop a substantial compiler-correctness proof in Rocq (Paraskevopoulou, 2026). PC2 can be instantiated in such systems provided that they faithfully represent the agreed definitions and obligations and supply a sound checker. The choice can therefore follow the application and the parties’ requirements, including the use of independent checkers to reduce reliance on a single implementation (Appendix B).

For our implementation, we chose Lean (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021). It combines a proof assistant with a programming language and a large mathematical library (The mathlib Community, 2020), allowing the contracts, obligations, proofs and Airlock program to be developed in one environment (Sec. 7). Lean has also attracted substantial recent work on AI-based autoformalization and theorem proving (Yang et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Agents using PC2 can draw on the resulting models, training data and proof-generation methods when preparing their calls. Lean’s existing automation can discharge routine arithmetic and finite-case obligations, while more difficult ones can be passed to an AI prover.

3  The Architecture

We introduce the formal definitions underpinning the architecture summarized in Sec. 2.

Notation

A predicate PP on a set XX gives, for each x∈Xx\in X, a statement P⁡(x)P(x) that holds or not; we identify PP with the set {x∈X∣P⁡(x)}\{x\in X\mid P(x)\}. A relation between sets XX and YY is a predicate on X×YX\times Y. A predicate is decidable if a program computes whether P⁡(x)P(x) holds. In general, predicates need not be decidable, and establishing that one holds may require a proof.

3.1  States and Tools

We denote by Σ\Sigma the space of states describing the aspects of the system relevant to the contract, such as files, credentials, account balances, messages, prices, and recorded assessments11 1 History-dependent constraints can be expressed by including the relevant history in the state description.. These may include both resources controlled by the Airlock and quantities that it can only observe. A state is a possible observation: what the tools would give about these aspects at a given instant. Actual readings, including those used by execution routines, are realizations of such observations. Different observations may describe the same world, and the same observation may be compatible with different worlds; Sec. 5.1 formalizes this relation. States provide the basis for specifying the contract and reasoning about the system’s evolution. The agent interacts with the system through tools (Yao et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2024).

Definition 1 (Tool).

A tool 𝖳{\mathsf{T}} over Σ\Sigma consists of an input space I𝖳I_{\mathsf{T}}, an execution routine exec𝖳\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}} operating on the system with inputs in I𝖳I_{\mathsf{T}}, and a transition model 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}, given by a relation on I𝖳×Σ×ΣI_{\mathsf{T}}\times\Sigma\times\Sigma.

An invocation exec𝖳​(i)\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}(i) performs the corresponding operation, such as sending an e-mail, downloading a file, or querying a database. Its behavior may depend on external responses or internal randomness, and the system may continue to evolve while the invocation runs.

The relation 𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}) specifies the states s′s^{\prime} admitted by the model during an invocation starting from ss, including its initial, intermediate, and final states. We introduce this model because reasoning about an operation does not require knowing its implementation in full: for example, a remote service may expose only an API specification. The model can remain coarse, admitting states that execution never reaches, as long as it admits the states that execution does reach from inputs and starting states permitted by the model. In Sec. 4 we discuss the conditions under which it covers execution sufficiently to support the guarantees.

Besides the operation’s own effects and every answer its services may give, the model must account for outside changes during the invocation: changes in what the tools would report that the operation does not cause. A price may change by at most a given amount per minute, mail may arrive, a hotel may cancel, and time advances. The model may also admit no state from some inputs and starting states, even when the routine itself could be invoked. This allows restrictions on authorization, as explained in Def. 3 and 3.5.2.

When a tool has no caller-supplied arguments, its input space is a singleton I𝖳={1}I_{\mathsf{T}}=\{1\}. We omit this unique input, writing 𝖣𝖳​(s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(s,s^{\prime}) for 𝖣𝖳​(1,s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(1,s,s^{\prime}) and exec𝖳​()\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}() for exec𝖳​(1)\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}(1).

The simplest tool is 𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾\mathsf{idle}, which leaves the system to itself: its input is a duration Δ\Delta, its routine waits for Δ\Delta without acting, and its model 𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾​(Δ,s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}}(\Delta,s,s^{\prime}) admits the states reached from ss by outside changes within at most Δ\Delta, ss itself included. We use it to design the control step (Sec. 3.5.1) and to account for the time between operations (Sec. 4.1).

3.2  Contract

Tools operate on the system, possibly changing its current state. A contract specifies the rules governing state changes and the use of tools.

Definition 2 (Contract).

A contract consists of a tuple 𝒦:=(Σ,𝖢,𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐,𝒯,ctrl,stop){\mathcal{K}}:=(\Sigma,\mathsf{C},{\mathsf{View}},\mathcal{T},\texttt{ctrl},\texttt{stop}), denoting the state space Σ\Sigma, a constraint predicate 𝖢\mathsf{C} on Σ\Sigma, a view function 𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐:Σ→𝒱{\mathsf{View}}:\Sigma\to{\mathcal{V}}, a collection 𝒯\mathcal{T} of tools available to the agent, a special tool ctrl with no caller-supplied arguments and available only to the system, and a decidable inactivity test stop:Σ→{true,false}\texttt{stop}:\Sigma\to\{\texttt{true},\texttt{false}\}. The test stop partitions Σ\Sigma into the inactive states Σstop:={s∈Σ:stop​(s)}\Sigma_{\mathrm{stop}}:=\{s\in\Sigma:\texttt{stop}(s)\} and the active states Σact:=Σ∖Σstop\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}:=\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{\mathrm{stop}}.

All formal constraints the parties aim to enforce in a contract 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} are contained in the predicate 𝖢\mathsf{C}, which identifies the region of states that comply with the contract; anything outside this region is considered a breach. For any s∈Σs\in\Sigma, the function 𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s){\mathsf{View}}(s) specifies the part of that state made visible to the agent, possibly hiding private information such as the contents of a document. Obtaining a state reading, and hence its view, may involve reading information held by the Airlock, querying external services, or combining several sources. The list 𝒯\mathcal{T} contains the tools the agent is allowed to invoke through the Airlock. The control tool ctrl is reserved for the Airlock and has two roles. As initializer, it starts the contract. A contract fixes no initial state, since nobody has observed the system when it is signed: it begins inactive, and when ctrl finds the system in a suitable inactive state, it moves it into an active state that satisfies 𝖢\mathsf{C}. As controller, it keeps the active contract compliant between admitted agent calls, while the agent prepares requests and their proofs are checked; depending on the contract, it may wait, take corrective action, or carry out a prescribed termination procedure. A contract is thus inactive before it starts and after it closes, and calls may be invoked only while the state belongs to Σact\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}.

where a state s=(x,t,ℓ)s=(x,t,\ell) contains the task information xx, the time tt, as the clock gives it, and a status ℓ\ell. The inactivity test is

stop​(x,t,ℓ):=ℓ≠𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀.\texttt{stop}(x,t,\ell)~:=~\ell\neq\mathsf{ongoing}.

Here 𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{pending} denotes that the contract is signed but not yet started, 𝗏𝗈𝗂𝖽\mathsf{void} that it never started, and 𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽\mathsf{terminated} that a safe state is met from which there is no interest to continue the contract (e.g. the contract arrived to expiration). A view and constraint may take the form

𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(x,t,ℓ):=(𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(x),t,ℓ),𝖢⁡(x,t,ℓ):=B⁡(x)∨ℓ≠𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀,{\mathsf{View}}(x,t,\ell):=({\mathsf{View}}(x),t,\ell),\qquad\mathsf{C}(x,t,\ell):=B(x)\,\vee\,\ell\neq\mathsf{ongoing},

where, with some abuse of notation, 𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐{\mathsf{View}} applied to Σ𝗍𝖺𝗌𝗄\Sigma_{\mathsf{task}} selects the visible task information, while BB collects the business constraints that need to hold at runtime, such as resource-accounting requirements. The contract is created 𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{pending}, and nothing is assumed about xx and tt.

A contract with a deadline dd must be closed by dd. For this guarantee, the time component tt records current time on the agreed timescale:

𝖢⁡(x,t,ℓ):=(B⁡(x)∧t≤d)∨ℓ≠𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀.\mathsf{C}(x,t,\ell):=\bigl(B(x)\wedge t\leq d\bigr)\vee\ell\neq\mathsf{ongoing}.

The states close to the deadline, from which idling could break this clause, belong to the region 𝐴𝑐𝑡\mathit{Act} of the control step, which terminates the contract there (Sec. 3.5.1).

The collection 𝒯\mathcal{T} contains tools for carrying out the task, and a tool 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle} that 1) determines whether a goal predicate 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(x,t,ℓ)=𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(x)\mathit{Goal}(x,t,\ell)=\mathit{Goal}(x) holds and 2) when called, its exec𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{settle}} performs an agreed settlement procedure between parties. For example, successful settlement transfers an escrow, records payment in the task information, and sets the status to ℓ=𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾𝖽\ell=\mathsf{settled}. In Sec. 3.5.2 we explain how the constraint and transition model make authorization require a proof of 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(x)\mathit{Goal}(x).

Here ctrl plays both roles, following the design of Sec. 3.5.1. As initializer, it starts the contract, setting ℓ=𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀\ell=\mathsf{ongoing}, if the escrow is in the Airlock’s custody, B⁡(x)B(x) holds and the deadline leaves enough time; otherwise it returns what the Airlock holds and sets ℓ=𝗏𝗈𝗂𝖽\ell=\mathsf{void}. As controller, in an ongoing session, it initiates termination when idling for one more period could leave less time than needed to close by the deadline. The termination routine performs the agreed operations, such as refunding the client, and sets ℓ=𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽\ell=\mathsf{terminated} upon completion. Otherwise, it idles before checking again. Section 3.5.1 illustrates a control design that also allows corrective actions.

Only 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle} runs the settlement procedure, and only ctrl the termination procedure. The label is held by the Airlock: no outside change modifies it, and only the routines of these two tools change it, each at its end. The routine of ctrl changes it from 𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{pending} to 𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{ongoing} or 𝗏𝗈𝗂𝖽\mathsf{void} when it initializes the contract, and from 𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{ongoing} to 𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽\mathsf{terminated} once it has run the termination procedure; the routine of 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle} changes it from 𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{ongoing} to 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾𝖽\mathsf{settled} once the settlement has succeeded.

The travel contract in Sec. 2.2 follows this template with the business constraints BB and goal given in its summary, retaining the budget bound in its clause at closing. Its deadline is 30 days after signing, and ctrl also terminates upon visa refusal, refunding the escrow in either case. The interpretation of expenditure commitments and confirmed bookings is developed in Sec. E.1 and E.2.

3.3  Obligations

The objective of the Airlock is to ensure that the system remains within 𝖢\mathsf{C} while the session is active, even if the agent behaves adversarially. This corresponds to enforcing daemonic control

Θ𝖳​(i,s):=∀s′∈Σ​𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′)⟹𝖢⁡(s′),\Theta_{{\mathsf{T}}}(i,s)~:=\quad\forall s^{\prime}\in\Sigma\;\;\;{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\;\implies\;\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}), (1)

to hold. This requires every state s′s^{\prime} admitted by 𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}) during the invocation to satisfy the clauses 𝖢⁡(s′)\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}). This is where 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} is used as a model of the actual behavior of exec𝖳\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}. A wrong model could invalidate safety in practice. Sec. 4 studies sufficient conditions for such a model to guarantee safety in real execution settings.

We also require enabledness, meaning that the model admits at least one state for the invocation:

Ξ𝖳​(i,s):=∃s′∈Σ.𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′).\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)~:=~\exists s^{\prime}\in\Sigma.\;{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}). (2)

Enabledness requires the call to belong to the domain covered by its model. The model may exclude an input or starting state even though the execution routine could still run there. Without this requirement, an excluded call would satisfy Θ𝖳​(i,s)\Theta_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s) vacuously and could be authorized without any guarantee about its effects. This is also how restrictions on authorization become preconditions in Sec. 3.5.2. Enabledness does not establish termination: 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} describes states during an invocation, including one that never returns.

We call their conjunction the admissibility condition for the call (𝖳,i)({\mathsf{T}},i) at state ss:

𝒜𝖳​(i,s):=Ξ𝖳​(i,s)∧Θ𝖳​(i,s).\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s):=\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\wedge\Theta_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s). (3)

In practice, an agent has access only to a view v∈𝒱v\in{\mathcal{V}} of the current state of the system. Admissibility must therefore hold at every state that could have generated v=𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s)v={\mathsf{View}}(s). Since calls are invoked only while the session is active and the obligation is intended to preserve compliance, we consider states in Σact\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}} that already satisfy the contract clauses 𝖢\mathsf{C}. This leads to the following notion of an obligation predicate. s\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}\;\;\;\bigl({\mathsf{View}}(s)=v\;\wedge\;\mathsf{C}(s)\bigr)\;\implies\;\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s). (4)

The obligation is thus the weakest precondition of the call for 𝖢\mathsf{C} (Dijkstra, 1975), taken over every state the agent cannot rule out (Appendix A).

Delayed obligations. The obligation above concerns a call starting from a state compatible with the observed view. Between obtaining that view and executing the call, however, other operations may change the system state. We would therefore like to establish that the call remains admissible after these operations, using the original view. Here we consider up to nn intervening invocations of ctrl, which will be useful for describing the Airlock core in Sec. 3.4. The resulting delayed obligation requires admissibility at every active state admitted by these control transitions; the delay counts control steps rather than elapsed time.

Definition 4 (Delayed obligation).

For s,s′∈Σacts,s^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}, set 𝖣ctrl⩽0​(s,s′):=(s=s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}^{\leqslant 0}(s,s^{\prime}):=(s=s^{\prime}) and define recursively, for n≥0n\geq 0,

𝖣ctrl⩽n+1​(s,s′):=𝖣ctrl⩽n​(s,s′)∨∃u∈Σact,𝖣ctrl⩽n​(s,u)∧𝖣ctrl​(u,s′).{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}^{\leqslant n+1}(s,s^{\prime}):={\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}^{\leqslant n}(s,s^{\prime})\ \vee\ \exists u\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}},\quad{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}^{\leqslant n}(s,u)\wedge{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(u,s^{\prime}). (5)

The first disjunct keeps the paths already admitted, and the second extends them by one control step. Thus 𝖣ctrl⩽n​(s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}^{\leqslant n}(s,s^{\prime}) describes the active states s′s^{\prime} admitted from ss by at most nn control steps through active states. For a tool 𝖳{\mathsf{T}}, input i∈I𝖳i\in I_{\mathsf{T}}, and view vv, the delayed obligation is

The call must therefore be admissible at every state in the control window of every compliant active state compatible with the view.

For n=0n=0, this recovers the ordinary obligation: Obl𝖳⩽0​(i,v)=Obl𝖳​(i,v)\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{T}}^{\leqslant 0}(i,v)=\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,v). The control model includes intermediate states as well as states at completion, so the recursion can impose admissibility at more states than actual invocation boundaries permit. This makes the condition conservative. The intervening control calls remain subject to their own obligation.

3.4  The Airlock Core

The preceding definitions describe the states over which a contract is expressed, the tools through which the agent acts on the system, and the constraints that its evolution must respect. The obligations specify what must be established before a requested tool call can be admitted. We now bring these components together in the Airlock proper: the system that reads the state and publishes views, checks the supplied proofs, and coordinates the execution of tool and control routines. The Airlock core execution loop is summarized in Alg. 1.

The Airlock acts on the system through two operations: the agent’s calls and the control step ctrl, which it runs by itself. Control also serves as an observer: its repeated invocations provide fresh readings while the agent prepares requests and their proofs are checked. The system may evolve between readings. The Airlock keeps a record of its latest reading and a log: an append-only list of the readings and accepted requests with their proofs, which both parties can read.

Delayed calls. Preparing a request and checking its proof take time, during which the state may change. The Airlock therefore uses the delayed obligation Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v)\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{T}}^{\leqslant n}(i,v) of Def. 4: the proof must establish admissibility after up to nn intervening control steps, counted from the view on which the request is based. Control continues while the request is prepared and checked. The current request can be executed once its proof is accepted, provided the session is still active and the allowance has not been exceeded. Figure 3 illustrates this sequence; Sec. 4 states the conditions under which it preserves compliance.

3.4.1  The Algorithm

The Airlock invokes agent tools and control sequentially: after invoking a routine, the execution loop resumes only when that invocation returns normally. Proof checking runs in parallel, allowing the Airlock to continue invoking ctrl while a request is prepared and checked. The system may change both during execution and between observations.

Each operation ends with a reading obtained by accessing the system; this reading becomes the record and is appended to the log. These end-of-operation readings are implicit in Alg. 1. Initially, the record is a reading of the state taken when the Airlock starts. The routine 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽​_​𝗏𝗂𝖾𝗐​()\mathsf{read\_view}() returns 𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s){\mathsf{View}}(s) for the recorded state ss, and 𝗂𝗌​_​𝖺𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗏𝖾​()\mathsf{is\_active}() evaluates 𝗇𝗈𝗍​stop​(s)\mathsf{not}~\texttt{stop}(s) on that record.

Initialization. The guarantees hold from the moment the contract starts, so the contract must start in a state that satisfies its clauses. The Airlock cannot assume such a state, since nobody has observed the system at signing, and it cannot check one, since 𝖢\mathsf{C} need not be decidable. The control step establishes it, in its role as initializer. The loop receives 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} and a certificate π𝒦\pi_{{\mathcal{K}}} with the evidence for all the assumptions on which the guarantees rest, as described in Sec. 6. The Airlock checks it with 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗍𝗋𝖺𝖼𝗍​_​𝖼𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄​(π𝒦,𝒦)\mathsf{contract\_check}(\pi_{{\mathcal{K}}},{\mathcal{K}}) and reads the state.

  1. (1)

    If the certificate is rejected, or the state is already active, the Airlock rejects the contract: it never takes over a running contract, whose compliance it could not vouch for.

  2. (2)

    Otherwise it runs one control step, in which ctrl acts as initializer: it either moves the system into an active state, which satisfies 𝖢\mathsf{C}, as the certificate proves, or leaves it inactive.

  3. (3)

    In the first case, we say that the contract starts, and the main loop begins. In the second, the contract never starts, and no call is ever made.

The agent plays no part in initialization: no view is published before the contract starts. The main loop exposes views and receives requests accompanied by proofs. Here, we describe these requests as a general interface, independently of how they are produced. However, in practice these are intended to be supplied by an agent.

Checking proofs. The initial contract check and the subsequent checks performed at runtime rely on mechanized reasoning, which allows mathematical statements and arguments to be expressed in a form that a computer can check (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021). The checker verifies that the supplied proof establishes the required statement. We leave the representation and construction of proofs implicit and describe which statements must be proved and when. Further details are given in Appendix B.

Main loop. After initialization, each cycle of Alg. 1 begins by checking whether the state is active. If so, the Airlock obtains v⁡[k]←𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽​_​𝗏𝗂𝖾𝗐​()v[k]\leftarrow\mathsf{read\_view}() and publishes (k,v⁡[k])(k,v[k]) through its output interface, making the view and its index available to the agent. Completed control steps provide the loop’s clock: the index kk counts these steps rather than elapsed time, v⁡[0]v[0] is the view at the start of the contract, and subsequent views are obtained after the corresponding control invocations. Recorded views are kept unchanged so that a request can identify the view on which its proof is based.

The Airlock then checks for requests without blocking. A request (𝖳,i,k0,n,π)({\mathsf{T}},i,k_{0},n,\pi) identifies the call, the recorded view v⁡[k0]v[k_{0}], the control-step allowance nn, and a proposed proof π\pi of the delayed obligation Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v⁡[k0])\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{T}}^{\leqslant n}(i,v[k_{0}]) from Def. 4. The allowance counts all control steps since that view, including those taken before the request arrives and during checking. The routine 𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗋𝗍​_​𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿​_​𝖼𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄\mathsf{start\_proof\_check} replaces any previous request and clears its verdict before starting the new check in parallel. It also checks that the tool and input are allowed and that the referenced view was published after the most recent agent call, so that only control steps intervene. The index k𝗅𝖺𝗌𝗍k_{\mathsf{last}} records that last call; its initial value −1-1 permits requests based on v⁡[0]v[0]. These checks are detailed in Appendix B.

If the current request’s proof has been accepted and k−k0≤nk-k_{0}\leq n, the Airlock invokes exec𝖳​(i)\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}(i) on the system as it then stands and waits for the routine to return. Agent tools are thus proof-gated. The delayed obligation requires admissibility at every active state admitted by the modeled control window. After the call, the Airlock records k𝗅𝖺𝗌𝗍=kk_{\mathsf{last}}=k and clears the accepted verdict through 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗎𝗆𝖾​_​𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿​()\mathsf{consume\_proof}(), so that the request authorizes only one invocation.

Finally, if the state is still active, the Airlock invokes execctrl​()\texttt{exec}_{\texttt{ctrl}}() and increments kk when control returns. Thus control runs in cycles with no admitted call and also follows an admitted call unless that call ends the session. The next cycle checks whether the state is still active before obtaining and publishing a new view. The upper part of Fig. 3 illustrates this sequence and the control steps counted by the allowance nn.

3.5  Tool design

The following examples illustrate how execution routines, transition models, and obligations fit together. We first give a possible design for the Airlock’s control tool, then consider families of agent tools and the constraints they can enforce.

3.5.1  The control tool ctrl

Consider a control routine that plays the two roles of Def. 2.

As initializer, it tests whether the system is in a decidable region 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦\mathit{Ready} of inactive states: those in which everything the contract needs at its start is in place, for instance the escrow in custody and the deadline ahead. There it runs exec𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{init}}, which initializes the contract: it moves the system into an active state that satisfies CC, for instance by recording the start time and setting a status to ongoing. From the other inactive states the routine leaves the contract inactive; a contract may record that it did not start, as Example 1 does with the label 𝗏𝗈𝗂𝖽\mathsf{void}.

As controller, it keeps the active contract in CC, as illustrated in Fig. 4(a). Fix an idle period pp and let CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}} be the set of states ss from which idling for one period remains in CC: C⁡(s′)C(s^{\prime}) holds for every s′s^{\prime} with 𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾​(p,s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}}(p,s,s^{\prime}). Like CC, the set CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}} need not be decidable, so the routine tests membership in a decidable region 𝐴𝑐𝑡⊇C∖Cidle\mathit{Act}\supseteq C\setminus C_{\mathrm{idle}}, which contains every compliant state from which idling may not be safe. In 𝐴𝑐𝑡\mathit{Act}, the control step cannot idle until the next operation, since the contract could break in the meantime: it must act, and by default it terminates the contract.

Optionally, termination can be avoided by a fixing routine exec𝖿𝗂𝗑\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{fix}} that, starting from a compliant state in a decidable region 𝐹𝑖𝑥\mathit{Fix}, remains in CC and, when it completes, leaves the system in CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}}. The routine then terminates only in 𝐸𝑛𝑑:=𝐴𝑐𝑡∖𝐹𝑖𝑥\mathit{End}:=\mathit{Act}\setminus\mathit{Fix}, where it must act but cannot fix.

The routine reads the state when it starts, its decision reading, and tests on it stop, 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦\mathit{Ready}, 𝐴𝑐𝑡\mathit{Act} and 𝐹𝑖𝑥\mathit{Fix}, all decidable:

𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐞​execctrl​():s←𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽​_​𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾​()𝐢𝐟​stop​(s)​𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧⊳initializer𝐢𝐟​s∈𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦​𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧​exec𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍​()𝐞𝐥𝐬𝐞​𝐢𝐟​s∉𝐴𝑐𝑡​𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧​exec𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾​(p)⊳controller𝐞𝐥𝐬𝐞​𝐢𝐟​s∈𝐹𝑖𝑥​𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧​exec𝖿𝗂𝗑​()𝐞𝐥𝐬𝐞​exec𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗍𝖾​().\begin{array}[]{l@{\qquad}l}\mathbf{routine}\ \texttt{exec}_{\texttt{ctrl}}():&\\ \qquad s\leftarrow\mathsf{read\_state}()&\\ \qquad\mathbf{if}\ \texttt{stop}(s)\ \mathbf{then}&\triangleright\ \textit{initializer}\\ \qquad\qquad\mathbf{if}\ s\in\mathit{Ready}\ \mathbf{then}\ \texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{init}}()&\\ \qquad\mathbf{else\ if}\ s\notin\mathit{Act}\ \mathbf{then}\ \texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{idle}}(p)&\triangleright\ \textit{controller}\\ \qquad\mathbf{else\ if}\ s\in\mathit{Fix}\ \mathbf{then}\ \texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{fix}}()&\\ \qquad\mathbf{else}\ \texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{terminate}}().&\end{array}

Here 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽​_​𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾​()\mathsf{read\_state}() accesses the system to obtain a state reading. The model 𝖣ctrl{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}} must cover the states encountered while reading and carrying out the selected action, including changes between the two. These choices make both roles safe, as the certificate must show (Sec. 4.1). As initializer, the routine makes the contract active only through exec𝗂𝗇𝗂𝗍\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{init}}, which ends in CC; elsewhere the contract stays inactive, provided that stop depends only on a status that the routines set, such as the label of Example 1. As controller, it idles only in CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}}, fixes only where fixing keeps CC, and otherwise terminates, which must also keep CC until the contract closes. Figure 4(a) illustrates the controller for 𝐴𝑐𝑡=C∖Cidle\mathit{Act}=C\setminus C_{\mathrm{idle}}. Panel (b) shows how it relates to delayed obligations: a call based on an earlier view must remain admissible throughout the region admitted by up to nn control steps. Further design choices and applications are discussed in Appendix C.

3.5.2  Agent tools

Preconditions. Given any tool 𝖳{\mathsf{T}}, and a predicate 𝖯𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Pre} over I𝖳×ΣI_{\mathsf{T}}\times\Sigma we can define a new tool 𝖳|𝖯𝗋𝖾{\mathsf{T}}|_{\mathsf{Pre}} with same input I𝖳|𝖯𝗋𝖾=I𝖳I_{{\mathsf{T}}|_{\mathsf{Pre}}}=I_{\mathsf{T}} and same execution exec𝖳|𝖯𝗋𝖾=exec𝖳\texttt{exec}_{{\mathsf{T}}|_{\mathsf{Pre}}}=\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}} but with restricted transition relation

D𝖳|𝖯𝗋𝖾​(i,s,s′):=𝖯𝗋𝖾⁡(i,s)∧D𝖳​(i,s,s′).D_{{\mathsf{T}}|_{\mathsf{Pre}}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\quad:=\quad\mathsf{Pre}(i,s)\,\wedge\,D_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}). (7)

The resulting effect of this restriction is that enabledness becomes equivalent to Ξ𝖳|𝖯𝗋𝖾​(i,s)⇔𝖯𝗋𝖾⁡(i,s)∧Ξ𝖳​(i,s)\Xi_{{\mathsf{T}}|_{\mathsf{Pre}}}(i,s)\iff\mathsf{Pre}(i,s)\wedge\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s) and the corresponding obligation is

Obl𝖳|𝖯𝗋𝖾​(i,v)⇔∀s∈Σact​(𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s)=v∧𝖢⁡(s))⟹(𝖯𝗋𝖾⁡(i,s)∧𝒜𝖳​(i,s)),\mathrm{Obl}_{{\mathsf{T}}|_{\mathsf{Pre}}}(i,v)~\iff\quad\forall s\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}\;\;\;\bigl({\mathsf{View}}(s)=v\;\wedge\;\mathsf{C}(s)\bigr)\;\implies\;\bigl(\mathsf{Pre}(i,s)\wedge\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\bigr), (8)

effectively adding 𝖯𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Pre} as a precondition gate that needs to be satisfied before allowing the original exec𝖳\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}} to be called. Thus authorization requires proving both the gate and preservation of the contract’s constraints at every compliant active state compatible with the view. The gate constrains the starting state ss, while Θ𝖳\Theta_{\mathsf{T}} requires compliance at every admitted s′s^{\prime}, including during execution. At states satisfying 𝖯𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Pre}, the original transition relation is unchanged, so any overapproximation property is preserved there. Below we consider an example where adding a precondition to a tool is particularly useful.

Settlement tools. As illustrated in Example 1, the 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle} tools provide the main avenue for a contract to specify 1) the task for which the Airlock is instantiated and 2) what should happen upon its completion. These tools combine a goal predicate 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathit{Goal} over Σ\Sigma with an execution routine exec𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{settle}} that performs the agreed settlement, such as releasing an escrow or delivering an artifact. Start with a tool 𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{free\_settle} that has no caller-supplied arguments and whose execution routine performs this settlement, then impose 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathit{Goal} as its precondition: 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾=𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾|𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathsf{settle}=\mathsf{free\_settle}|_{\mathit{Goal}}. Its model includes states during settlement, such as a payment in progress, as well as completed or failed outcomes. Suppose the contract certificate establishes that 𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{free\_settle} is admissible at every compliant active state where 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathit{Goal} holds. The obligation then reduces to

Obl𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(v)⟺∀s∈Σact.(𝖢⁡(s)∧𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s)=v)⟹𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s),\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{settle}}(v)~\Longleftrightarrow~\forall s\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}.\;\bigl(\mathsf{C}(s)\wedge{\mathsf{View}}(s)=v\bigr)\implies\mathit{Goal}(s), (9)

namely that 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle}’s obligation holds exactly when every compliant active state compatible with the view satisfies the goal. In particular, when goal achievement can be determined by v=𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s)v={\mathsf{View}}(s) alone, we have Obl𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s))⟺𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s)\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{settle}}({\mathsf{View}}(s))\Longleftrightarrow\mathit{Goal}(s) for any active state ss satisfying C⁡(s)C(s). For a delayed call, the goal must hold at every active state admitted by the control window. Preservation during settlement must already have been established in the certificate: for example, the clauses must allow a payment in progress, accounting for funds in transit, rather than only its final 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾𝖽\mathsf{settled} state.

Expert tools. Some clauses in the contract depend on judgments that the parties cannot readily express as a formal predicate: whether a document meets a requirement, an image shows a defect, or a hotel is suitable. The parties can instead agree on an expert to make these assessments. The tool’s routine exec𝖾𝗑𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗍\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{expert}} invokes the “expert”: this can be an LLM with a fixed prompt specified by the contract to extract information from a document or assess its contents, and records the answer. A vision model or human reviewer can play the same role. The model 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} covers the states while the assessment is pending and the possible recorded answers, as well as costs or disclosures incurred by consulting the expert. For example, a contract might reserve parts of the state to record the results of an expert’s calls to be used later on during task execution. In the travel contract, a booking requires a recorded hotel rating of at least 7; a pending assessment provides no such evidence. Recorded verdicts can be reused via memoization for the same object and evidence to avoid repeated sampling. Expert tools thus allow contracts to combine formal conditions with assessments of unstructured information and qualitative requirements.

Communication tools. E-mails, document uploads, and messages between agents add to a history of exchanges. A contract may constrain the recipient, the content disclosed, or the conditions under which a message may be sent. As a simple example, consider a tool 𝗌𝖾𝗇𝖽\mathsf{send} with input space I𝗌𝖾𝗇𝖽=𝐷𝑜𝑐×𝑅𝑒𝑐I_{\mathsf{send}}=\mathit{Doc}\times\mathit{Rec}, whose routine exec𝗌𝖾𝗇𝖽​(d,r)\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{send}}(d,r) sends document dd to recipient rr. Let 𝑆𝑒𝑛𝑡⁡(s)\mathit{Sent}(s) record the document–recipient pairs disclosed so far, including partial disclosures. If no other disclosures occur during the call, a simple model is

𝖣𝗌𝖾𝗇𝖽​((d,r),s,s′):=𝑆𝑒𝑛𝑡⁡(s)⊆𝑆𝑒𝑛𝑡⁡(s′)⊆𝑆𝑒𝑛𝑡⁡(s)∪{(d,r)}.{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{send}}((d,r),s,s^{\prime})\quad:=\quad\mathit{Sent}(s)\subseteq\mathit{Sent}(s^{\prime})\subseteq\mathit{Sent}(s)\cup\{(d,r)\}. (10)

This admits both states before disclosure and states in which some or all of dd has been disclosed to rr, whether or not delivery eventually succeeds. Let the contract constrain disclosure by 𝖢⁡(s):=𝑆𝑒𝑛𝑡⁡(s)⊆𝐴𝑙𝑙𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑑\mathsf{C}(s):=\mathit{Sent}(s)\subseteq\mathit{Allowed}. Assuming the state space admits the updated record for every state and input, 𝗌𝖾𝗇𝖽\mathsf{send} is enabled and, at a compliant active state ss, its obligation reduces to

Obl𝗌𝖾𝗇𝖽((d,r),𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐(s))⇔(d,r)∈𝐴𝑙𝑙𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑑.\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{send}}((d,r),{\mathsf{View}}(s))\quad\iff\quad(d,r)\in\mathit{Allowed}. (11)

More detailed models can distinguish which contents are disclosed and through which routes; a failed delivery does not undo information already disclosed.

Query tools. A query tool performs operations such as web searches, database queries, and measurements. Its routine exec𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{query}} issues a query qq and records the response with its source and, where relevant, time or version. Information exposed through the resulting view can support subsequent proofs: in the travel contract, a booking confirmation from the agreed service may provide evidence for goal achievement. Starting from a general tool 𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒\mathsf{query}, each contract can impose its own restrictions through 𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒|𝖯𝗋𝖾\mathsf{query}|_{\mathsf{Pre}}, retaining the same input space and execution routine. For example, a contract may require queries not to modify the queried data and to respect a spending limit BB:

𝖯𝗋𝖾⁡(q,s):=𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽𝖮𝗇𝗅𝗒⁡(q)∧(𝗌𝗉𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡(s)+κ⁡(q)≤B).\mathsf{Pre}(q,s):=\mathsf{ReadOnly}(q)\wedge\bigl(\mathsf{spent}(s)+\kappa(q)\leq B\bigr). (12)

Here 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽𝖮𝗇𝗅𝗒⁡(q)\mathsf{ReadOnly}(q) expresses the first requirement and 𝗌𝗉𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡(s)\mathsf{spent}(s) is cumulative expenditure. The bound κ⁡(q)\kappa(q) applies throughout execution: every state s′s^{\prime} admitted by 𝖣𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒​(q,s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{query}}(q,s,s^{\prime}) satisfies 𝗌𝗉𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡(s′)≤𝗌𝗉𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡(s)+κ⁡(q)\mathsf{spent}(s^{\prime})\leq\mathsf{spent}(s)+\kappa(q), including while waiting for a response or after failure. By 8, the proof must establish this gate together with admissibility at every compliant active state compatible with the view.

The model must include states before a response is available, partial responses, errors, and timeouts as well as successful completion. Enabledness only requires that some state is admitted; it guarantees neither completion nor a successful answer. In particular, a timeout does not establish that no matching record exists. Records support only the claims justified by the model: a response may describe a particular database version, returned text need not be true, and reported availability is not a reservation. Read-only queries may still incur costs or disclose information, and the queried data may change independently during the call; these changes must also be modeled.

4  Guarantees

Section 3 presented the structure of PC2 and the obligations governing tool execution. We now study the guarantees that follow from this structure. We first show that the state satisfies 𝖢\mathsf{C} at every instant, regardless of the requests and proposed proofs supplied to the Airlock (Sec. 4.1). Section 5 relates the state to the world it describes and identifies conditions under which compliance implies safety.

4.1  Anytime compliance to the contract

Given a contract 𝒦:=(Σ,𝖢,𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐,𝒯,ctrl,stop){\mathcal{K}}:=(\Sigma,\mathsf{C},{\mathsf{View}},\mathcal{T},\texttt{ctrl},\texttt{stop}), we identify sufficient conditions for the state to satisfy 𝖢\mathsf{C} at every instant of the execution of Alg. 1, for arbitrary incoming requests and proposed proofs.

For a given execution, we write s⁡(τ)s(\tau) for the possibly unobserved state of the system at time τ\tau, in the sense of Sec. 3. As described in Sec. 3.4, the Airlock invokes control and tool routines sequentially. Each execution interval starts when a routine is invoked and ends when it returns, or continues indefinitely if it does not return. During this interval the state may change through the routine’s actions and outside changes (see Fig. 3).

We begin with the proof checks introduced in Sec. 3.4. Before executing a requested tool call, the Airlock forms its obligation from the contract and the published view, and passes it, together with the supplied proof, to the checker: a program that checks whether the supplied argument establishes the required statement according to the rules of a fixed logic. For our implementation, we choose dependent type theory as the underlying logic: it provides a common language for the contract’s data, statements, and proofs, with proof checking reduced to type checking. A statement is represented by a type, and the checker verifies that the supplied proof is an expression of that type. In Lean, used for our mechanization (Sec. 7), this check is performed by the Lean kernel (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021).

Assumption A1 (Sound checking).

For any proof π\pi and statement Φ\Phi, if the proof-checker accepts π\pi as a proof of Φ\Phi, then Φ\Phi holds under the axioms and interpretation of the chosen logic.

A1 is independent of the choice of proof assistant. The checker must use the contract’s agreed definitions and permitted axioms. Accepting a proof of Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v)\mathrm{Obl}_{{\mathsf{T}}}^{\leqslant n}(i,v) then establishes that obligation, allowing the analysis below to rely on it regardless of how the proof was produced. The obligation, however, is expressed in terms of the transition models 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} and 𝖣ctrl{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}, while the state evolves through the execution routines and the outside changes. To apply the proof to execution, the models must cover every state that execution can reach. We denote these possibilities by the effect relation E𝖳E_{\mathsf{T}} on I𝖳×Σ×ΣI_{\mathsf{T}}\times\Sigma\times\Sigma: E𝖳​(i,s,s′)E_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}) holds if and only if an invocation of exec𝖳​(i)\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}(i) starting in ss can reach s′s^{\prime} during its execution. This includes initial, intermediate and final states, outside changes during the invocation, and states reached if the routine never returns.

Assumption A2 (Coverage of state transitions).

For every 𝖳∈𝒯∪{ctrl}{\mathsf{T}}\in{\cal T}\cup\{\texttt{ctrl}\},

∀i∈I𝖳,s,s′∈ΣΞ𝖳​(i,s)∧E𝖳​(i,s,s′)⟹𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′).\forall i\in I_{\mathsf{T}},\;s,s^{\prime}\in\Sigma\qquad\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\wedge E_{{\mathsf{T}}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\implies{\mathsf{D}}_{{\mathsf{T}}}(i,s,s^{\prime}). (13)

A2 requires 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} to over-approximate these possibilities wherever Ξ𝖳​(i,s)\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s) holds: it may admit states through which the state never passes, but must include every state through which it may pass during the operation, not only the one at its end. The restriction to enabled calls due to Ξ𝖳\Xi_{\mathsf{T}} allows 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} to exclude inputs and starting states, as in the precondition construction of Sec. 3.5.2; the obligation then prevents authorization of those calls. The Airlock uses 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} to form obligations and does not need to know E𝖳E_{\mathsf{T}}. The role of E𝖳E_{\mathsf{T}} in the analysis is to specify the behavior that the model must cover for these proofs to apply to execution. Both relations concern the state; Sec. 5 and 6 discuss how a deployment’s routines, services and host support this coverage and the state’s correspondence with the world.

The obligation preserves compliance from a state that already satisfies 𝖢\mathsf{C}. To apply it throughout the loop, the loop must start from a compliant state, and the control step, which the Airlock runs by itself, must preserve compliance too. Nobody has observed the system at signing, so its initial state is not known to comply. The Airlock does not assume it: the contract begins inactive, and the control step, as initializer, makes it active only in a compliant state.

Assumption A3 (Initialization and control).

The control tool satisfies

∀s∈Σact\displaystyle\forall s\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}} 𝖢​(s)⟹𝒜ctrl​(s),\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{C}(s)\implies\mathcal{A}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s), (controller)
∀s∈Σstop,s′∈Σact\displaystyle\forall s\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{stop}},\ s^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}} 𝖣ctrl​(s,s′)⟹𝖢⁡(s′),\displaystyle\qquad{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s,s^{\prime})\implies\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}), (initializer)

and it is enabled at every inactive state: Ξctrl​(s)\Xi_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s) for every s∈Σstops\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{stop}}.

The two lines are the two roles of ctrl. As controller, from a compliant active state, it passes only through compliant states. As initializer, from an inactive state, it can make the contract active only in a compliant state. Both are certified once, at startup (Sec. 3.4), so no new proof is required at each cycle, and the second replaces the assumption that the initial state complies, which nobody could check. Enabledness makes A2 applicable to every control step as well as to calls.

Finally, the argument relies on the Airlock running Alg. 1 as specified.

Assumption A4 (Execution integrity).

Execution follows Alg. 1 and the proof-checking routine in Appendix B. In particular:

  1. (i)

    execution is a sequence of contiguous operations, each a tool call or a control step: the first starts when the Airlock has read the state, and each of the others when the previous one ends;

  2. (ii)

    after each routine returns, the current state is read and appended to the log; views and the inactivity test are computed from this reading, and initially from a reading taken when the Airlock starts;

  3. (iii)

    a call runs only for the pending request (𝖳,i,k0,n,π)({\mathsf{T}},i,k_{0},n,\pi), at most once, if no other call ran since v⁡[k0]v[k_{0}] was published, in an iteration kk with k0≤k≤k0+nk_{0}\leq k\leq k_{0}+n, and after the proof-checking routine in Appendix B has checked that 𝖳∈𝒯{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}, that i∈I𝖳i\in I_{\mathsf{T}}, and that π\pi proves Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v⁡[k0])\mathrm{Obl}_{{\mathsf{T}}}^{\leqslant n}(i,v[k_{0}]), a statement the Airlock forms itself;

lets us follow the operations one after another: the state at the end of one is also the state at the start of the next. In practice, between two operations the Airlock reads the state, publishes a view and invokes the next routine, which takes microseconds, while requests take seconds to prepare. Proof checking runs in parallel with control, so the state need not remain fixed while a proof is checked. Appendix D discusses executions with bounded gaps between routines.

connects execution to the information used by the loop. After each routine, the Airlock records the current state. Whenever it publishes a view or tests whether the session is still active, it uses the latest reading. Thus these decisions reflect the result of the routine that just ran.

Together, ensure that the latest recorded state is the state from which the next routine starts. Part (iii) then connects that invocation to its authorization: the checked proof concerns the requested tool and input, and the call runs only within its control window, with no intervening tool call or reuse of the request.

A request may refer to a view published several control steps before its call starts. To apply its delayed obligation, we must show that the actual starting state is among those covered by that obligation. The following lemma connects the request’s counter window to the states admitted by 𝖣ctrl⩽n{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}^{\leqslant n}.

Lemma 1 (Window).

Assume A2, A3 and A4. Let a call run for the request (𝖳,i,k0,n,π)({\mathsf{T}},i,k_{0},n,\pi) from state s′s^{\prime}, and let s¯\bar{s} be the state from which v⁡[k0]v[k_{0}] was computed. If 𝖢\mathsf{C} holds at every instant from the start of the contract to the invocation, then s¯\bar{s} and s′s^{\prime} are active and 𝖣ctrl⩽n​(s¯,s′){\mathsf{D}}^{\leqslant n}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(\bar{s},s^{\prime}).

Proof.

Let kk be the iteration in which the call runs. By , k0≤k≤k0+nk_{0}\leq k\leq k_{0}+n, and only control invocations intervene between s¯\bar{s} and the call’s starting state s′s^{\prime}. There are m=k−k0≤nm=k-k_{0}\leq n such invocations. By , they are contiguous, and their final states are the recorded readings. For m=0m=0, s¯=s′\bar{s}=s^{\prime}. The loop computes a view and starts an iteration only from a reading that it has found active (). So s¯\bar{s}, the starting state of each of these control steps, and s′s^{\prime} are active. Each control step started from a compliant state by hypothesis, since it runs after the contract has started. Hence A3 gives its enabledness, and A2 places its final state in 𝖣ctrl{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}} from its starting state. Chaining these steps through active states gives 𝖣ctrl⩽m​(s¯,s′){\mathsf{D}}^{\leqslant m}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(\bar{s},s^{\prime}), hence 𝖣ctrl⩽n​(s¯,s′){\mathsf{D}}^{\leqslant n}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(\bar{s},s^{\prime}), since m≤nm\leq n and each window contains the previous one (Def. 4). ∎

The lemma explains why the state need not remain unchanged after a view is published: given compliance up to the call, its delayed obligation covers the actual starting state despite the intervening control steps. The window bounds the number of those steps, not the elapsed time.

Theorem 1 (Anytime compliance to the contract).

Under A1, A2, A3 and A4, for any sequence of tool-call requests and proposed proofs supplied to Alg. 1, every resulting execution in which the contract starts satisfies 𝖢\mathsf{C} at every instant from the start until the contract closes, closing included, or at every instant after the start if it never closes.

Proof.

By , operations are contiguous. Let s0s_{0} be the state when the Airlock starts. Initialization runs a control step from s0s_{0}, which is inactive, since otherwise the Airlock rejects the contract (A4). By A3 the control step is enabled at s0s_{0}, so A2 places the state s1s_{1} at its end in 𝖣ctrl​(s0,⋅){\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s_{0},\cdot). Since the contract starts, s1s_{1} is active, and A3 gives 𝖢⁡(s1)\mathsf{C}(s_{1}). It therefore suffices to prove, by induction on the invocations after the start, that each starts in a compliant state and preserves compliance throughout its execution. The first starts from s1s_{1}. Consider an operation that starts from the state ss, with 𝖢⁡(s)\mathsf{C}(s) by induction; ss is active, since Alg. 1 runs operations only from such states.

(1) A control step. A3 gives 𝒜ctrl​(s)\mathcal{A}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s), that is Ξctrl​(s)\Xi_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s) and Θctrl​(s)\Theta_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s). Every state s′s^{\prime} reached during its interval satisfies Ectrl​(s,s′)E_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s,s^{\prime}), so A2 gives 𝖣ctrl​(s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s,s^{\prime}), hence 𝖢⁡(s′)\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}).

(2) A call 𝖳⁡(i){\mathsf{T}}(i), for the request (𝖳,i,k0,n,π)({\mathsf{T}},i,k_{0},n,\pi). By , the checker accepted π\pi as a proof of Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v⁡[k0])\mathrm{Obl}_{{\mathsf{T}}}^{\leqslant n}(i,v[k_{0}]), which therefore holds by A1. Let s¯\bar{s} be the state from which v⁡[k0]v[k_{0}] was computed: 𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s¯)=v⁡[k0]{\mathsf{View}}(\bar{s})=v[k_{0}], and 𝖢⁡(s¯)\mathsf{C}(\bar{s}) by induction. By Lemma 1, s¯\bar{s} and ss are active and 𝖣ctrl⩽n​(s¯,s){\mathsf{D}}^{\leqslant n}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(\bar{s},s). The obligation, applied to s¯\bar{s} and ss, gives 𝒜𝖳​(i,s)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s), that is Ξ𝖳​(i,s)\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s) and Θ𝖳​(i,s)\Theta_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s). Every state s′s^{\prime} reached during the call’s interval satisfies E𝖳​(i,s,s′)E_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}), so A2 gives 𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}), hence 𝖢⁡(s′)\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}).

In both cases, compliance holds throughout the invocation. If it returns, its final state is compliant and, by , it is the state from which the next operation, if any, starts. If it never returns, the same argument applies throughout its continuing execution. A rejected or expired request authorizes no call. The argument makes no assumption about how requests or proofs are produced. ∎

Theorem 1 derives compliance of the whole execution from the individual obligations. What, then, does each obligation require? By Def. 4, Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v)\mathrm{Obl}_{{\mathsf{T}}}^{\leqslant n}(i,v) holds exactly when the call is admissible from every active state admitted by at most nn control steps, through active states, from a compliant active state with view vv. It therefore accounts both for information hidden by the view and for changes during the control window. This condition is relative to the chosen models, which may admit states and paths that actual execution cannot follow. Establishing admissibility from all these states suffices for compliance, but a false obligation need not imply that the call would actually violate the contract. Relative to the models, nothing weaker would do: every rule that safely admits calls on the basis of the view implies the obligation, so the agent may follow any strategy whose calls keep the contract (Proposition A.1).

The theorem allows arbitrary requests and proposed proofs, but its coverage assumption still concerns every state that execution can reach, including through outside interactions. Section 5.2 examines how restricting the agent’s access can make this assumption easier to establish while retaining models that allow useful calls.

4.2  Completion through goal tools

A standard contract (Example 1) ends in one of three ways: it is void if the conditions to start do not hold, settled when the agent proves its goal, or terminated by the control step, for instance at its deadline with a refund. The following theorem shows that it ends in at most one of them, and in each only as agreed; Thm. 5 adds that, with a deadline, it does end. Besides A1, A2, A3 and A4, the theorem uses that the settlement tool is 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾=𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾|𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathsf{settle}=\mathsf{free\_settle}|_{\mathit{Goal}} (Sec. 3.5.2), that the control step terminates the contract exactly when its decision reading is in the region 𝐸𝑛𝑑\mathit{End} of Sec. 3.5.1, and the properties of the label stated in Example 1.

Theorem 2 (Completion).

Assume A1, A2, A3 and A4. In every execution of Alg. 1 with a standard contract, the contract ends in at most one of the following ways:

  1. (1)

    void: the conditions to start did not hold; the execution never starts and no tool-call is made;

  2. (2)

    settled: the agreed settlement procedure ran, from a state where the goal held;

  3. (3)

    terminated: the agreed termination procedure ran, after a control step found a termination condition.

Proof.

The contract is created pending, and only the routines of ctrl and 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle} change the label, at their end (Example 1). The first operation is a control step, which, as initializer, sets the label to 𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{ongoing} when its decision reading is in 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦\mathit{Ready}, and to 𝗏𝗈𝗂𝖽\mathsf{void} otherwise; in the second case the loop stops, and no call is made. Once the label is 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾𝖽\mathsf{settled} or 𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽\mathsf{terminated}, the contract is inactive and Alg. 1 runs no further operation, so the contract ends in at most one way. (2) As in case (2) of the proof of Thm. 1, the checker accepted a proof of Obl𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾⩽n​(v⁡[k0])\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{settle}}^{\leqslant n}(v[k_{0}]), which therefore holds (A1). Admissibility of 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle} includes its enabledness, hence 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathit{Goal}, by the precondition construction, at every active state of the window, and Lemma 1 places in the window the state from which the settlement started. (3) The label becomes 𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖽\mathsf{terminated} only when the control step has run the termination procedure, which it does exactly when its decision reading is in 𝐸𝑛𝑑\mathit{End}. ∎

The case analysis rests on the code of the Airlock and of the control step; case (2) also rests on the checker and on the obligation of 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle}.

At the call-selection step of an active cycle, a pending settlement request whose proof has been accepted and whose window remains valid is selected for execution without further authorization. The client therefore has no discretionary veto over an authorized settlement through the Airlock. The next proposition identifies exactly what its proof must establish.

Proposition 1 (What settlement asks).

Assume A3 for the standard contract, and let its certificate establish that 𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{free\_settle} is admissible at every compliant active state where 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathit{Goal} holds. Then, for every view vv and delay nn,

Obl𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾⩽n​(v)⇔∀s,s′∈Σact(𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐⁡(s)=v∧𝖢⁡(s)∧𝖣ctrl⩽n​(s,s′))⟹𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s′).\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{settle}}^{\leqslant n}(v)\iff\forall s,s^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}\quad\bigl({\mathsf{View}}(s)=v\wedge\mathsf{C}(s)\wedge{\mathsf{D}}^{\leqslant n}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s,s^{\prime})\bigr)\implies\mathit{Goal}(s^{\prime}).
Proof.

By the precondition construction, Ξ𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′)⇔𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s′)∧Ξ𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′)\Xi_{\mathsf{settle}}(s^{\prime})\iff\mathit{Goal}(s^{\prime})\wedge\Xi_{\mathsf{free\_settle}}(s^{\prime}) and Θ𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′)⇔(𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s′)⟹Θ𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′))\Theta_{\mathsf{settle}}(s^{\prime})\iff\bigl(\mathit{Goal}(s^{\prime})\implies\Theta_{\mathsf{free\_settle}}(s^{\prime})\bigr). From left to right, 𝒜𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{settle}}(s^{\prime}) gives Ξ𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′)\Xi_{\mathsf{settle}}(s^{\prime}), hence 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s′)\mathit{Goal}(s^{\prime}). From right to left, 𝖢⁡(s′)\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}) holds, since s′s^{\prime} is reached from the compliant state ss by control steps from active states, which preserve 𝖢\mathsf{C} by A3. Together with 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s′)\mathit{Goal}(s^{\prime}), the certificate gives 𝒜𝖿𝗋𝖾𝖾​_​𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{free\_settle}}(s^{\prime}), hence 𝒜𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾​(s′)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{settle}}(s^{\prime}). ∎

When every compliant active state with the given view satisfies the goal and modeled control steps preserve it throughout the window, the right-hand side holds. A proof of this condition suffices for authorization while the request remains valid; admissibility of the settlement procedure is already established by the contract certificate.

5  From compliance to safety

Section 4 establishes that execution remains within the contract’s constraints. We now study when this compliance protects the resources and interactions the contract concerns. A payment recorded within budget, for instance, does not establish that the service charged no additional fees. Connecting the two requires both a mathematical account of what the state describes and conditions on the system that produces and acts on that description. This is the gap between a specification, which a machine can be built to meet, and a requirement about the world in which the machine operates (Jackson, 1995; Zave and Jackson, 1997). A proof relates a system to a model of it, never the model to the world (Smith, 1985).

Three questions guide this section and the next:

  • •

    What does the mathematical construction guarantee? Under which assumptions does compliance of the state imply safety in the world?

  • •

    How can those assumptions be established for a deployment? What must the routines, host, access controls and external services do, and what evidence supports these claims?

  • •

    What do the parties do about what remains assumed? Which assumptions do they accept, who undertakes responsibility for them, and what happens if they fail?

Section 5.1 addresses the first question, and illustrates on an example what a world is. Section 5.2 studies how isolating the agent supports useful effect models and guarantees that apply to every agent under the same deployment conditions. Section 5.3 discusses the requirements on execution. Section 6 addresses the second and third questions. It shows that the assumptions of a deployment need not be established from scratch, since they follow by composing guarantees that ship with the capability modules from which its tools are built (Sec. 6.1). It then assembles these dependencies in a tree and records their proposed allocation to parties (Sec. 6.5), connecting this analysis to the treatment of remaining assumptions in Sec. 8.3.

5.1  World safety

Let 𝒲\mathcal{W} be a space of configurations of the relevant system and environment, including such facts as actual charges, issued payment instructions and the state of external services. We write w⁡(τ)w(\tau) for its configuration at time τ\tau. A relation ρ⊆𝒲×Σ\rho\subseteq\mathcal{W}\times\Sigma specifies how the contract’s state describes these facts: ρ⁡(w,s)\rho(w,s) means that ss is a valid description of ww. This description can be partial or conservative. A recorded upper bound on expenditure, for instance, can describe several different amounts actually charged, and the same expenditure can admit several valid bounds. In the terms of program refinement, ρ\rho is an abstraction relation between the world and its description (Hoare, 1972; Abadi and Lamport, 1991). It thus differs from 𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐{\mathsf{View}}, which determines what the requesting agent sees of the state.

Example 2 (A trading agent and its world).

Consider an agent that manages a small investment portfolio. Its tools read and send email, read and write files in a working directory, search, read and publish posts on a social network, read quotes from a market-data service, query a database of past transactions, and place orders through a brokerage account. A world w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W} is a configuration of all these systems: the messages in the mailbox and those delivered to their recipients, the files on disk, the posts that the public can read, the prices at which the securities currently trade, the rows of the database, and the cash, positions and pending orders held by the broker, together with the current time. The state ss records only what the contract needs, as the tools report it: for instance, the messages sent with their recipients, the posts published, the last quote read with its time, and the money committed to orders. The correspondence ρ\rho says what each record means in the world. The record of sent messages describes the world if every message that left the mailbox appears in it. A recorded quote describes the world if the service reported that price at that time, whatever the price is now. The recorded commitment may be a conservative bound, counting each pending order at its maximum cost. A protection such as “never commit more than a given amount, and never disclose the portfolio publicly” is a predicate 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} on worlds: it concerns the money actually committed and what the public can actually read, not the records. Much of the world changes without the agent: messages arrive, prices move, other applications update the database, and the broker executes pending orders.
