In most scenarios, such as the example above, viewing a world w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W} as a single object is impractical. This is because applications are often organized in largely independent systems, so the resulting world can be naturally represented as a product of their configurations, 𝒲=𝒲mail×𝒲files×⋯×𝒲broker\mathcal{W}=\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{mail}}\times\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{files}}\times\dots\times\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{broker}}, and the state a product of the corresponding records. In Sec. 6 we will address this question and show how a world, a state, a correspondence and the tools that act on them can be assembled from small modules, each concerning a single service such as the mailbox or the brokerage account, whose guarantees are established once.

Let 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} be a predicate on 𝒲\mathcal{W} specifying the intended protection, as in Example 2 above. Worlds may include history when the protection concerns past events, such as a document having been disclosed, as history variables do in proofs of refinement (Abadi and Lamport, 1991). Compliance is expressed by 𝖢⁡(s)\mathsf{C}(s), while safety concerns 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w)\mathsf{Safe}(w). We connect them through two conditions. Fidelity requires the state to remain a valid description of the world as execution proceeds. Adequacy requires a world described by a compliant state to satisfy the intended safety property. Together, they relate what the Airlock enforces on states to what the parties require of the world. This is the satisfaction argument of requirements engineering, in which a specification, together with properties of the world, entails a requirement (Zave and Jackson, 1997; Jackson, 2001).

Fidelity. To express preservation of correspondence, we must account for how the world and state evolve together. Let E^𝖳​(i,w,s,w′,s′)\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}) hold when an invocation of exec𝖳​(i)\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}(i) starting in (w,s)(w,s) can reach (w′,s′)(w^{\prime},s^{\prime}) at any instant of its execution. This includes outside changes during the invocation and applies also to a routine that does not return. The effect relation of Sec. 4.1 is its projection on states:

E𝖳(i,s,s′)⇔∃w,w′∈𝒲.E^𝖳(i,w,s,w′,s′).E_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\quad\iff\quad\exists w,w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}.\;\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}). (14)

This joint relation lets us state what it means for execution to preserve the description: starting from a pair satisfying ρ\rho, every pair reached during an enabled invocation must still satisfy it, as a simulation relation is preserved by every step of the system it relates (Lynch and Vaandrager, 1995). Correspondence must also be established when the contract starts, since nothing is known of the world when the contract is signed. We collect these requirements in the following assumption.

Assumption A5 (Fidelity).

For every 𝖳∈𝒯∪{ctrl}{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{\texttt{ctrl}\}, input i∈I𝖳i\in I_{\mathsf{T}}, worlds w,w′w,w^{\prime} and states s,s′s,s^{\prime},

ρ⁡(w,s)∧Ξ𝖳​(i,s)∧E^𝖳​(i,w,s,w′,s′)⟹ρ⁡(w′,s′),\rho(w,s)\wedge\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\wedge\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime})\quad\implies\quad\rho(w^{\prime},s^{\prime}), (15)

and, for every inactive state ss and active state s′s^{\prime},

E^ctrl​(w,s,w′,s′)⟹ρ⁡(w′,s′).\widehat{E}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime})\quad\implies\quad\rho(w^{\prime},s^{\prime}). (16)

A2 requires the model to cover the states reached during execution, while A5 requires those states to remain valid descriptions of the world. The claim that a service reported a confirmed booking at time tt describes a past event. Once established, it survives a later cancellation if the record is preserved and the world model retains that history. A claim that the booking is currently confirmed must instead account for possible cancellations. Fidelity thus depends on what the recorded information means, while adequacy asks whether that meaning suffices for the intended protection. The second line is the counterpart of the initializer line of A3: the control step makes the contract active only in a state that describes the world, whatever the world was before, so nothing needs to be assumed about the world when the contract is signed. For the control design of Sec. 3.5.1, a sufficient condition is that 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽​_​𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗍𝖾​()\mathsf{read\_state}() returns a state that describes the world when the reading completes, and that the remaining initialization preserves this correspondence until the contract becomes active.

Adequacy. Fidelity gives meaning to the state throughout execution. We must then ask whether the clauses imposed on that state suffice for the protection the parties require: even a faithful description can satisfy a contract that omits an important constraint. An agent that optimizes within the clauses pushes exactly where they and the intended protection come apart (Manheim and Garrabrant, 2018), and no contract specifies everything its parties care about (Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield, 2019).

Assumption A6 (Adequacy).

For every w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W} and s∈Σs\in\Sigma,

ρ⁡(w,s)∧𝖢⁡(s)⟹𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w),\rho(w,s)\wedge\mathsf{C}(s)\quad\implies\quad\mathsf{Safe}(w), (17)

and, for a contract with a goal 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙\mathit{Goal} whose intended outcome in the world is a predicate 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙𝒲\mathit{Goal}_{\mathcal{W}},

ρ⁡(w,s)∧𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s)⟹𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙𝒲​(w).\rho(w,s)\wedge\mathit{Goal}(s)\quad\implies\quad\mathit{Goal}_{\mathcal{W}}(w). (18)

For specified ρ\rho, 𝖢\mathsf{C} and 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe}, A6 can be proved when the relationships expressed by the correspondence and clauses imply the required protection. In the payment ledger of Appendix E, correspondence bounds actual expenditure by recorded reservations, and the clause bounds those reservations by the budget, so adequacy follows by arithmetic. The parties must also establish that 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} expresses their intended protection, since a proof of the implication alone does not settle this question.

We can now extend Thm. 1 from compliance of the state to safety in the world. The additional step is to show that the state is a valid description of the world throughout execution from the start of the contract, including while a routine runs.

Theorem 3 (World safety).

Under A1, A2, A3, A4, A5 and A6, every execution of Alg. 1 in which the contract starts satisfies 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w⁡(τ))\mathsf{Safe}(w(\tau)) at every instant from the start until the contract closes, closing included, or at every instant after the start if it never closes, for any sequence of requests and proposed proofs.

Proof.

By Thm. 1, 𝖢⁡(s⁡(τ))\mathsf{C}(s(\tau)) holds from the start of the contract. When the control step starts the contract, the state describes the world, by the second line of A5. Each later operation is enabled at its starting state: control by A3, and a requested call by its accepted obligation and Lemma 1, as in the proof of Thm. 1. Hence the first line of A5 preserves correspondence throughout that operation, which, operations being contiguous (), lasts until the next one starts, or throughout its continuing execution if it never returns. Induction over the operations therefore gives ρ⁡(w⁡(τ),s⁡(τ))\rho(w(\tau),s(\tau)) at every instant from the start. Together with compliance, A6 yields the conclusion. ∎

Theorem 3 separates what must be checked for each call from what must be established about the deployment. The checker reasons about the contract’s states and tool models. Fidelity keeps these states valid descriptions throughout execution, and adequacy makes their compliance sufficient for safety in the world. The argument transfers a property from the description to the world it describes, as a refinement mapping transfers a property proved of a specification to a system that implements it (Abadi and Lamport, 1991). This is what allows the local obligations to protect the resources and interactions the contract concerns.

Establishing these conditions requires examining which interactions the deployment permits, and Sec. 5.2 considers how the agent’s access affects them.

Many contracts also prescribe a settlement action once a goal has been achieved, as in the standard contract of Example 1. The completion guarantee of Thm. 2 concerns this goal as expressed on states. The following corollary transfers it to the intended outcome 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙𝒲\mathit{Goal}_{\mathcal{W}} in the world, through ρ\rho and the second part of A6.

Corollary 4 (Completion in the world).

Under the assumptions of Thm. 2, assume A5 and A6. Then every invocation of the settlement routine starts at an instant τ\tau satisfying 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙𝒲​(w​(τ))\mathit{Goal}_{\mathcal{W}}(w(\tau)).

Proof.

As in the proof of Thm. 2, case (2), the accepted settlement obligation gives 𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙⁡(s⁡(τ))\mathit{Goal}(s(\tau)). By the correspondence argument in the proof of Thm. 3, ρ⁡(w⁡(τ),s⁡(τ))\rho(w(\tau),s(\tau)) holds, and 18 gives the conclusion. ∎

A central question is to determine when assumptions A5 and A6 are satisfied. Appendix E works through step-by-step examples where they are derived in practice, for a payment ledger for safety and booking confirmations for completion, including settlement of the travel contract.

5.2  Complete mediation and sandboxing: safety against every agent

The agent’s access. The discussion so far has left one actor implicit: the agent, which may be adversarial. Suppose that the agent could act on the state or on the world independently of the Airlock, for instance by deleting or sending messages in a mailbox while a tool that reads the mailbox is running. Since E𝖳E_{\mathsf{T}} and E^𝖳\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}} describe everything that can happen during an invocation of 𝖳{\mathsf{T}}, they would then include the agent’s direct actions, alongside the outside changes of the world. The possible effects can therefore depend on which agent is present. We write E𝖳αE^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}} and E^𝖳α\widehat{E}^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}} for the effect relations of 𝖳{\mathsf{T}} when the agent is α\alpha. Coverage (A2) requires each model 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} to cover these additional changes, and fidelity (A5) requires the correspondence to survive them. One option is to model the particular agent, tying the justification of the tools to that agent’s behaviour. The other is to use a common model that covers every change any agent could cause. This avoids verifying the agent, but if those possibilities include a contract violation during every invocation, no call can be authorized, and control itself cannot satisfy A3.

An agent can also change the world without changing the state. If that change invalidates what the state describes, fidelity fails, and enlarging 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} alone cannot repair it. Figure 5 illustrates these failures, and Appendix F works through them in detail. The classical answer to this problem is to restrict the agent’s access instead of modeling it. This is sufficient, though, as we discuss at the end of this section, not necessary.

Controlling access in this way has a long history in computer security. In particular, the principle of complete mediation requires each access to the objects that a system protects to pass through the authorization that governs it (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975). Here the protected objects are the state and the world, and the authorization is the proof gate: the Airlock checks an obligation before executing a requested operation (). Mediation is complete only if the agent has no other way to act, which is what isolation, stated below, provides. The Airlock then acts as a reference monitor for the agent’s access (Anderson, 1972).

To express what this restriction provides, we take the agent to comprise every process that runs for it: a model, the code that drives it, and any process they start. We then fix a tool 𝖳{\mathsf{T}} and its input ii, and consider its routine running with that input while none of the agent’s processes runs. Other parties, external services and the passage of time remain present, under the same conditions on their behaviour. We call these reference executions. As with the effect relations of Sec. 4.1 and 5.1, E𝖳∙​(i,s,s′)E^{\bullet}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}) holds when such an invocation starting in ss can reach s′s^{\prime} at any instant, and E^𝖳∙​(i,w,s,w′,s′)\widehat{E}^{\bullet}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}) records the corresponding possibility for a world–state pair. The following assumption specifies how the agent can be present without introducing effects beyond those of these executions.

Assumption A7 (Isolation of the agent).

The agent acts on the system only through invocations selected by the Airlock among its requests, in particular:

  1. (i)

    Nothing else it does, through any channel (e.g. files, network connections, shared memory or messages to other processes) changes the world, the state or the internal state of a running routine, during or between invocations of any 𝖳∈𝒯∪{ctrl}{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{\texttt{ctrl}\} routine.

  2. (ii)

    Each tool or ctrl routine receives from the agent only the call input, fixed at invocation.

  3. (iii)

    The evolution of the world and the state during the invocation depends only on their current values, the routine’s internal state and the fixed input. In particular it does not depend on the agent’s computation or internal state.

The assumption concerns how the system is organized, rather than whether the agent behaves cooperatively. It allows the agent to choose requests and prepare proofs, but excludes both direct changes to the protected system and further influence on a running routine through shared data or pending requests. The independence condition lets us compare an execution with an agent to one of the reference executions. The prototypical way to establish A7 is to run the agent in a sandbox, a container or lightweight virtual machine (Goldberg et al., 1996; Agache et al., 2020) with no network route, except to its model provider if the contract allows it, and no access to the Airlock’s files, memory or credentials, which stay with the routines. The implementation is documented in the GitHub repository.

Lemma 2 (Isolation).

Under isolation (A7), for every agent α\alpha, adversarial or not, for every 𝖳∈𝒯∪{ctrl}{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{\texttt{ctrl}\}, and all inputs, worlds and states,

E𝖳α​(i,s,s′)⟹E𝖳∙​(i,s,s′),E^𝖳α​(i,w,s,w′,s′)⟹E^𝖳∙​(i,w,s,w′,s′).E^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\implies E^{\bullet}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}),\qquad\widehat{E}^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime})\implies\widehat{E}^{\bullet}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}).

Consequently, coverage and fidelity established for the reference executions imply A2 and A5 for every agent.

Proof.

Fix an agent α\alpha. Consider an execution in which the agent α\alpha runs, and in it an invocation of 𝖳{\mathsf{T}} on input ii that starts in the world ww and the state ss. For each instant τ\tau of the invocation, write w⁡(τ)w(\tau), s⁡(τ)s(\tau) and r⁡(τ)r(\tau) for the world, the state and the internal state of the routine at τ\tau. By A7, nothing the agent does changes these three quantities, and how they can evolve depends only on their current values and on ii, not on the agent. The trajectory τ↦(w⁡(τ),s⁡(τ),r⁡(τ))\tau\mapsto(w(\tau),s(\tau),r(\tau)) is therefore one that a reference execution, started in ww and ss with the same input, can also produce. Every pair (w⁡(τ),s⁡(τ))(w(\tau),s(\tau)) is thus reached in a reference execution, which proves the implication for E^𝖳α\widehat{E}^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}}, and projecting on states gives it for E𝖳αE^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}}. Coverage and fidelity for the reference executions therefore apply to every pair reached in the actual execution. ∎

For a stepwise account of this argument, Appendix G states sufficient conditions under which the agent’s computation can be removed while preserving the worlds and states that an invocation can reach. Host and service activity remain possible in the reference executions. The argument uses non-interference, which studies whether the activity of one process can affect another (Goguen and Meseguer, 1982; Rushby, 1992).

The lemma allows us to establish coverage and fidelity by studying the tool together with the services and outside interactions that remain possible when the agent cannot act directly. These conditions then apply to the calls of any agent that uses the system through the Airlock. Combined with the earlier results, they give the guarantees of PC2 for every agent, which Sec. 5.4 states together (Thm. 5).

Under these conditions, changing the agent does not require a new argument about the effects of each tool. The argument still depends on the tool, its input, the host and the external services, whose properties must continue to hold. In Sec. 6.1 we will use this separation when studying how guarantees for individual capability modules can support the tools of different contracts.

Isolation is sufficient for this conclusion, but safety does not require prohibiting every interaction outside the Airlock. An agent may retain direct access to a service’s API or permission to modify a shared record, provided all effects possible through that access are covered by the models and preserve the required properties, without relying on the agent to choose its actions responsibly. Conversely, removing the agent’s direct access does not resolve unsafe behaviour by a service or another party: protecting a resource against them is the role of custody, which applies complete mediation to the resource rather than to the agent (Prop. 2). The construction is particularly applicable when the system already limits how resources can change, and isolation prevents the agent from bypassing those limits.

5.3  Execution and duration of the guarantees

The correspondence arguments above explain how records can remain meaningful as routines and services act on the world. To combine these arguments with internal coherence, we must also establish that the deployed checker, control routine and execution loop behave as required in Sec. 4.1. This brings us back to A1, A2, A3 and A4. In particular, protecting the proof gate includes protecting the checker and contract, the recorded views, and the association between a proof and the tool and input that actually run. For example, replacing the input after its proof is checked breaks the connection required by A4, even if the checker itself is sound. The deployed routines must also satisfy the models used to form obligations: A2 covers every state encountered during execution, including outside changes, and A3 requires control to preserve compliance from every compliant active state. Verification must therefore concern the routines that run, under the service and host conditions used to establish these properties. The loop and checker are documented in the GitHub repository (Sec. 7).

Pauses and timing. A pause during a routine is part of that routine’s execution interval. Any changes while it is paused must be covered by its model under A2 and preserve correspondence under A5. If unrestricted pauses make these properties false, the deployment needs an appropriate bound or protection that remains effective during the pause, such as a lease that expires unless the Airlock renews it (Gray and Cheriton, 1989). For bounded gaps between routines, see Appendix D. A control window bounds the number of control steps rather than elapsed time.

Duration and completion. Theorem 3 guarantees safety up to closing, and throughout a non-closing execution. It does not imply that a pending request is eventually executed or that settlement succeeds. These are liveness properties, while the guarantees are safety properties (Alpern and Schneider, 1985), the class that a mechanism checking each step can enforce (Schneider, 2000). A deadline is the exception: written as a clause of the contract (Example 1), it is a safety property, and Thm. 5(4) obtains it from anytime compliance, independently of whether the agent makes progress. Likewise, the absence of a further approval before an authorized settlement call (Sec. 4.2) requires the deployment to hold the authority needed to issue it. That authority does not guarantee that the service completes the transfer. Responsibility for unmet conditions and possible remedies are separate matters, discussed in Sec. 8.

Some protections outlast the contract. In the payment ledger of Appendix E, the reservations recorded at closing still bound the charges that arrive afterwards, without the Airlock continuing to run, as long as no new instruction can be issued and the provider keeps respecting its limits.

5.4  The guarantees of PC2

We now state the guarantees of PC2 together, in the world and for every agent.

Theorem 5 (The guarantees of PC2).

Assume A1, A3, A4, A7 and A6, and A2 and A5 for the reference executions. Then every execution of Alg. 1 satisfies the following, for every agent and every sequence of requests and proofs.

  1. (1)

    Anytime safety. 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} holds in the world at every instant from the start of the contract until it closes, or at every instant after the start if it never closes.

Moreover, if the contract is in standard form (Example 1), it ends in at most one of the three ways of Thm. 2, and:

  1. (2)

    Settlement. If it is settled, the goal held in the world when the settlement started.

  2. (3)

    Termination. If it is terminated, a control step found a termination condition.

  3. (4)

    Deadline. If it has a deadline dd and starts, either settlement or termination is initiated by dd.

Proof.

We follow the guarantees from the agent to the world.

Every agent. By isolation (A7) and Lemma 2, every effect of a routine, in an execution with any agent, is also an effect of a reference execution. Coverage and fidelity established for the reference executions therefore give A2 and A5 for every agent, and requests and proofs may be arbitrary.

The clauses. The checker accepts only true obligations (A1), the models cover what the routines do (A2), the control step starts the contract compliant and keeps it compliant (A3), and a call runs only for an accepted proof, within its window (A4). These are the hypotheses of Thm. 1, so 𝖢\mathsf{C} holds at every instant from the start.

The world. When the control step starts the contract, the state describes the world, and every later operation preserves this description (A5), so the state describes the world at every instant from the start (Thm. 3). A world described by a compliant state is safe (A6, first part). This gives (1).

How the contract ends. In standard form, only the routines of ctrl and 𝗌𝖾𝗍𝗍𝗅𝖾\mathsf{settle} change the label, and the loop stops once the contract is inactive (A4), so the contract ends in at most one of the three ways (Thm. 2). If it is settled, the accepted proof of the settlement call gives the goal on the state when settlement starts (Thm. 2); the state then describes the world, and a world described by a state with the goal satisfies the goal in the world (A6, second part). This gives (2), as in Cor. 4. If it is terminated, the control step terminated it only from a decision reading in 𝐸𝑛𝑑\mathit{End}. This gives (3).

The deadline. If the contract has a deadline dd, every ongoing state has t≤dt\leq d by the clauses. Since tt records current time on the agreed timescale, the contract cannot remain ongoing after dd. The label changes only at the end of the settlement or termination routine, so the routine that closed the contract must have started by dd. This gives (4). ∎

6  Composing guarantees

Sections 4 and 5 have described the guarantees through abstract objects: states, tool models, effects and correspondences with the world. In an application, these objects describe concrete routines, records and services, such as Example 2 or the payment ledger and booking service described in Appendix E. Constructing these descriptions and their proofs anew for every contract would require substantial repeated work, with repeated opportunities to omit an effect or a condition on the service. Much of this work concerns the available operations rather than the particular agreement. The discipline of recording a payment instruction before issuing it, for example, can support contracts with different budgets and goals.

We propose to organize this work in reusable capability modules. A module can be developed as a software component whose routines come with state descriptions, tool models, a correspondence with the world and guarantees under stated conditions. A contract can then be built from a combination of these modules, reusing their routines and arguments while specifying the constraints of the particular agreement. Reuse requires preserving the conditions under which the modules were verified, and their combination may require additional arguments. The purpose of this section is to show how such a process can work through a few constructions and examples, rather than to give an exhaustive account of capability composition.

In Sec. 6.1 we define capability modules and explain how to combine them into a state space and a collection of tools on which to build a contract. We give conditions under which their coverage and fidelity guarantees establish A2 and the first line of A5 for the combined tools. The contract still requires its own arguments for the start, the control step and adequacy, alongside the conditions on the checker and execution mechanism. In Sec. 6.5 we bring these arguments together to identify what must be established about the routines, host and services used by a particular contract, and who can provide evidence for it. This produces a tree in which an implication from more specific conditions to a claim is a refinement.

6.1  Capability modules

A contract may use several services, each described by different state fields and a different correspondence to the world. For instance, a contract that makes payments and obtains booking confirmations can combine a payment ledger with a record of confirmations. While a booking request runs, earlier payments may still produce charges. Each module must therefore account both for its own operations and for what can happen while none of them runs. We represent the latter by an idle tool.

Definition 5 (Capability module).

A capability module is a tuple M=(𝒲M,ΣM,ρM,𝒯M,𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M)M=(\mathcal{W}_{M},\Sigma_{M},\rho_{M},\mathcal{T}_{M},\mathsf{idle}_{M}), where 𝒲M\mathcal{W}_{M} and ΣM\Sigma_{M} are sets, ρM\rho_{M} is a relation on 𝒲M×ΣM\mathcal{W}_{M}\times\Sigma_{M}, and 𝒯M\mathcal{T}_{M} is a set of tools over ΣM\Sigma_{M} whose routines operate on the system described by 𝒲M\mathcal{W}_{M}. The tool 𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M∈𝒯M\mathsf{idle}_{M}\in\mathcal{T}_{M} has no caller-supplied input and waits without intervening. Its effects describe the changes possible during intervals in which no other routine of MM runs.

Several modules M1,…,MnM_{1},\ldots,M_{n} can supply the state space of a contract, for example by taking Σ=∏k=1nΣMk\Sigma=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\Sigma_{M_{k}} and building its tools from their operations, as we describe below.

Here 𝒲M\mathcal{W}_{M} describes the resource and the services relevant to its operations, while ΣM\Sigma_{M} contains the quantities through which the contract reasons about them. These quantities may be protected records, such as the ledger, or current observations, such as a price the tools would report if asked. An observation of the current price may change while the module waits. A stored quotation remains unchanged, but its correspondence must then describe the quotation and its validity, rather than identify it with the current price. This is the distinction between a possible observation and a recorded reading made in Sec. 3.

𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M\mathsf{idle}_{M} and ctrl. The tool 𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M\mathsf{idle}_{M} describes what may happen while the module waits without intervening. This can be specified independently of a contract, whereas the contract’s reserved tool ctrl must preserve its particular clause 𝖢\mathsf{C} and respond to its termination conditions. A contract might use a local control routine, say execctrlM\texttt{exec}_{\texttt{ctrl}_{M}}, when the necessary intervention depends only on the module’s state. In other cases the decision requires information from several modules: whether to release a payment can depend on a booking and a deadline. Such a decision may require a routine operating on the combined state. We therefore include 𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M\mathsf{idle}_{M} in every module without requiring a local controller.

Local guarantees. Coverage and fidelity can first be established for each module separately. Write E𝖳E_{\mathsf{T}} and E^𝖳\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}} for its tools’ state and joint world–state effects, as in Sec. 4.1 and 5.1, with all states and worlds now belonging to that module. For each 𝖳∈𝒯M{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}_{M}, define

𝖢𝗈𝗏M​(𝖳)\displaystyle\mathsf{Cov}_{M}({\mathsf{T}})\ :⇔∀i,s,s′Ξ𝖳(i,s)∧E𝖳(i,s,s′)⟹𝖣𝖳(i,s,s′),\displaystyle:\iff\ \forall i,s,s^{\prime}\quad\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\wedge E_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\implies{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}), (19)
𝖥𝗂𝖽M​(𝖳)\displaystyle\mathsf{Fid}_{M}({\mathsf{T}})\ :⇔∀i,w,s,w′,s′ρM(w,s)∧Ξ𝖳(i,s)∧E^𝖳(i,w,s,w′,s′)⟹ρM(w′,s′),\displaystyle:\iff\ \forall i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}\quad\rho_{M}(w,s)\wedge\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\wedge\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime})\implies\rho_{M}(w^{\prime},s^{\prime}), (20)

with the quantifiers ranging over the tool’s inputs and the module’s spaces. These are the routine conditions of A2 and A5 for one module. For idle, fidelity applies to waiting intervals from states where its model is enabled. Under A7, these guarantees can be established using the reference effects of Sec. 5.2: Lemma 2 then makes them applicable to every agent.

For example, whoever implements a payment module can prove that its routine records an instruction before sending it, subject to stated conditions on who can change the ledger and use the payment credentials. Another contract can reuse that proof when it uses the same routine under the same conditions. In Sec. 6.3 we give three constructions that make these conditions explicit.

6.2  Composing capability modules

To build an environment suited to an application, we need to combine modules that provide its different operations and descriptions of the world. For example, a travel application can draw on payment and booking modules, then add an operation relating a purchase to its payment. We consider two constructions, illustrated in Fig. 6. A product puts the modules’ world and state descriptions together and makes their existing tools available on the combined state. An extension adds fields, correspondence conditions or routines involving those components. We first describe how tools on separate modules can be combined, since this is used in both constructions.

Paired tools. Let U∈𝒯M1U\in\mathcal{T}_{M_{1}} and V∈𝒯M2V\in\mathcal{T}_{M_{2}}, where the modules have disjoint world and state coordinates. We write U⊗VU\otimes V for a tool over ΣM1×ΣM2\Sigma_{M_{1}}\times\Sigma_{M_{2}} with input space IU×IVI_{U}\times I_{V}. When both components are non-idle, its routine executes them concurrently in a single invocation and returns when both have returned. If one component is idle, it waits until the other returns. Pairing two idle tools gives an operation that waits on both components. The model is

𝖣U⊗V​((i1,i2),(s1,s2),(s1′,s2′))⇔𝖣U​(i1,s1,s1′)∧𝖣V​(i2,s2,s2′).{\mathsf{D}}_{U\otimes V}\bigl((i_{1},i_{2}),(s_{1},s_{2}),(s^{\prime}_{1},s^{\prime}_{2})\bigr)\iff{\mathsf{D}}_{U}(i_{1},s_{1},s^{\prime}_{1})\wedge{\mathsf{D}}_{V}(i_{2},s_{2},s^{\prime}_{2}). (21)

Compatibility of effects. Reusing the separate tools’ guarantees requires checking that their combination does not introduce effects outside those for which the guarantees were established. Write i=(i1,i2)i=(i_{1},i_{2}), w=(w1,w2)w=(w_{1},w_{2}) and s=(s1,s2)s=(s_{1},s_{2}), and similarly for primed quantities. The required condition, for all such inputs and coordinates, is

E^U⊗V​(i,w,s,w′,s′)⟹E^U​(i1,w1,s1,w1′,s1′)∧E^V​(i2,w2,s2,w2′,s2′).\widehat{E}_{U\otimes V}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime})\implies\widehat{E}_{U}(i_{1},w_{1},s_{1},w^{\prime}_{1},s^{\prime}_{1})\wedge\widehat{E}_{V}(i_{2},w_{2},s_{2},w^{\prime}_{2},s^{\prime}_{2}). (22)

The condition concerns the whole paired invocation. If one routine finishes before the other, its effects and guarantees must also cover the remaining wait. When V=𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M2V=\mathsf{idle}_{M_{2}}, running UU must leave all changes on the second module within its idle effects, and conversely for an idle first component. Disjoint coordinates therefore need not mean that the resources are unaffected by each other. For example, a merchant may charge an earlier payment instruction while a booking call runs, provided the payment module’s idle effects account for it. If an interaction introduces changes outside a component’s effects, its description and guarantees must be revised, or the interacting parts must be treated together.

This is the question addressed by rely–guarantee reasoning: the conditions under which one component was verified must be respected by the other components and their environment (Jones, 1983; Abadi and Lamport, 1995). Here 22 states that requirement directly for the effects used in our coverage and fidelity arguments.

Product. A product makes each module’s tools available while accounting for changes on the other modules as they wait. For payment and booking modules, a payment call becomes 𝗉𝖺𝗒⊗𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗄\mathsf{pay}\otimes\mathsf{idle}_{\mathsf{book}}: its model includes the payment routine’s effects and the changes that the booking can undergo during the payment.

Definition 6 (Product modules).

For modules M1,M2M_{1},M_{2} with disjoint world and state coordinates, their product M=M1⊗M2M=M_{1}\otimes M_{2} has 𝒲M=𝒲M1×𝒲M2\mathcal{W}_{M}=\mathcal{W}_{M_{1}}\times\mathcal{W}_{M_{2}}, ΣM=ΣM1×ΣM2\Sigma_{M}=\Sigma_{M_{1}}\times\Sigma_{M_{2}} and

ρM​((w1,w2),(s1,s2))⇔ρM1​(w1,s1)∧ρM2​(w2,s2).\rho_{M}((w_{1},w_{2}),(s_{1},s_{2}))\iff\rho_{M_{1}}(w_{1},s_{1})\wedge\rho_{M_{2}}(w_{2},s_{2}).

Its tools are

𝒯M={𝖳1⊗𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M2:𝖳1∈𝒯M1}∪{𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M1⊗𝖳2:𝖳2∈𝒯M2}.\mathcal{T}_{M}=\{{\mathsf{T}}_{1}\otimes\mathsf{idle}_{M_{2}}:{\mathsf{T}}_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{M_{1}}\}\ \cup\ \{\mathsf{idle}_{M_{1}}\otimes{\mathsf{T}}_{2}:{\mathsf{T}}_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{M_{2}}\}. (23)

The idle tool is 𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M1⊗M2=𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M1⊗𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M2\mathsf{idle}_{M_{1}\otimes M_{2}}=\mathsf{idle}_{M_{1}}\otimes\mathsf{idle}_{M_{2}}.

The product is associative and commutative up to the canonical regrouping and permutation of coordinates: M1⊗(M2⊗M3)≅(M1⊗M2)⊗M3M_{1}\otimes(M_{2}\otimes M_{3})\cong(M_{1}\otimes M_{2})\otimes M_{3} and M1⊗M2≅M2⊗M1M_{1}\otimes M_{2}\cong M_{2}\otimes M_{1}. These identifications preserve the correspondence and tool models and retain the same component routines. We can therefore write M1⊗⋯⊗MnM_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes M_{n} without parentheses for any finite nonempty family of modules with pairwise disjoint coordinates.

Extension. Applications may also require records that relate several modules or operations that coordinate their use, for example by chaining calls or executing them concurrently. An extension can add these operations together with new state fields and a correspondence describing what those fields mean. Making the additions explicit identifies what must be established beyond the guarantees already supplied by the modules.

Definition 7 (Extension modules).

Let MM be a module, ZZ a nonempty set, ρ′\rho^{\prime} a relation on 𝒲M×ΣM×Z\mathcal{W}_{M}\times\Sigma_{M}\times Z, and 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime} a set of tools over ΣM×Z\Sigma_{M}\times Z. The extension N=ext⁡(M,Z,ρ′,𝒯′)N=\operatorname{ext}(M;Z,\rho^{\prime},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}) has 𝒲N=𝒲M\mathcal{W}_{N}=\mathcal{W}_{M}, ΣN=ΣM×Z\Sigma_{N}=\Sigma_{M}\times Z and

ρN​(w,(s,z))⇔ρM​(w,s)∧ρ′​(w,s,z).\rho_{N}(w,(s,z))\iff\rho_{M}(w,s)\wedge\rho^{\prime}(w,s,z).

Its tools are {𝖳~:𝖳∈𝒯M}∪𝒯′\{\widetilde{{\mathsf{T}}}:{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}_{M}\}\cup\mathcal{T}^{\prime}. Each retained tool 𝖳~\widetilde{{\mathsf{T}}} has the same inputs and routine as 𝖳{\mathsf{T}}, leaves zz unchanged and has model

𝖣𝖳~​(i,(s,z),(s′,z′))⇔𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′)∧z′=z.{\mathsf{D}}_{\widetilde{{\mathsf{T}}}}(i,(s,z),(s^{\prime},z^{\prime}))\iff{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\wedge z^{\prime}=z. (24)

The idle tool is 𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M~\widetilde{\mathsf{idle}_{M}}, and the fields in ZZ change only through the added routines.

We write ext⁡(M)\operatorname{ext}(M) when the added state, correspondence and tools are understood. This denotes a chosen extension of MM, whose identity depends on those additions. In particular, ext⁡(M1⊗M2)\operatorname{ext}(M_{1}\otimes M_{2}) in Fig. 6 extends the product of the two modules.

For example, a travel application can extend the payment and booking modules with a register ZZ of completed purchases. Each entry identifies an order, its booking confirmation and its payment instruction. The added correspondence ρ′\rho^{\prime} states that the identified confirmation and instruction were issued for that order, relating the two modules’ histories to the new record. An added purchase routine obtains a confirmation, issues the associated payment and records their association. This uses all three parts of an extension: additional state, a relation connecting it to the world, and an operation involving several modules. This instantiates the extension in Fig. 6: the added routine chains the booking and payment calls and stores their association in zz. The new record can remain unchanged when the original tools run, but its correspondence must remain true. We return to that requirement in Sec. 6.4.

An extension can also add an operation alone, taking ZZ to be a singleton and ρ′\rho^{\prime} to be true. One example is the paired tool 𝖳1⊗𝖳2{\mathsf{T}}_{1}\otimes{\mathsf{T}}_{2} with both components non-idle, which the product alone does not provide. It runs both routines concurrently as one Airlock invocation. Its conjunction model and the compatibility requirement are those already given in 21 and 22.

Another example is a tool whose implementation runs 𝖳1{\mathsf{T}}_{1} while a controller maintains the second component. A requester submits this combined operation to the proof gate, and the controller runs as part of its implementation. This does not grant access to the contract’s reserved ctrl, which the Airlock alone invokes between requested calls. Writing the combined tool as 𝖳1⊗ctrl2{\mathsf{T}}_{1}\otimes\texttt{ctrl}_{2} is appropriate only when such a controller can be specified for the second component and its guarantees cover the whole invocation. When the necessary decisions depend on several components, the added routine must instead use the full state.

Building a contract. A product, possibly extended as above, gives a module NN on which we can build the contract of Def. 2. We take Σ=ΣN\Sigma=\Sigma_{N}, select from 𝒯N\mathcal{T}_{N} the tools exposed through 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and supply the clause 𝖢\mathsf{C}, view 𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐{\mathsf{View}}, reserved control tool ctrl and termination test stop. The tool ctrl and any other required tools absent from NN can be added by extension. For modules M1,…,MnM_{1},\ldots,M_{n} and additional fields ZZ, the resulting state space is Σ=(∏k=1nΣMk)×Z\Sigma=(\prod_{k=1}^{n}\Sigma_{M_{k}})\times Z. The clause need not split into separate conditions on the components: it may, for example, require each payment instruction to have an associated booking confirmation. The obligations of Sec. 3 use this combined state, clause and tool models without modification.

The spaces 𝒲N\mathcal{W}_{N} and correspondence ρN\rho_{N} provide the interpretation used in Sec. 5.1. The composition result in Sec. 6.4 explains when the modules’ guarantees establish coverage and fidelity for the contract’s tools. The requirements on ctrl in A3, as initializer and as controller, must still be proved for its chosen clause, as must the adequacy implication ρN​(w,s)∧𝖢⁡(s)⟹𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w)\rho_{N}(w,s)\wedge\mathsf{C}(s)\implies\mathsf{Safe}(w). The checker and execution mechanism remain subject to A1 and A4.

6.3  Three capability constructions

We now give concrete conditions under which a module satisfies its local guarantees. The constructions in Tab. 1 distinguish a protected record of instructions, a record of what a service reported, and a description of quantities that may change independently. They can be combined when a resource requires more than one of these arguments.

Custody. Consider a payment account whose credentials are kept by the Airlock. Its payment routine can send the provider an instruction specifying a recipient and a spending limit, with an identifier distinguishing it from other instructions. Before sending the message, the routine adds the instruction to a protected register. This order matters because the provider may charge the account as soon as it receives the message, before any acknowledgement returns. We want the register to account for every instruction that the provider can act on, including those still in progress. This is the part of the payment-ledger argument in Appendix E that concerns custody of the authority to issue payments. The bound on the charges themselves additionally depends on the provider respecting each instruction’s limit.

Let 𝐼𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟\mathit{Instr} be the set of these payment instructions, ΣM\Sigma_{M} the set of its finite subsets, and I𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾=𝐼𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟I_{\mathsf{issue}}=\mathit{Instr}. A state ss is the register. Write J⁡(w)J(w) for the history of submitted instructions, including pending instructions from the moment of submission. Define

ρM​(w,s)\displaystyle\rho_{M}(w,s) ⇔∀j∈J⁡(w).j∈s,\displaystyle\iff\forall j\in J(w).\ j\in s, (25)
𝖣𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾​(j,s,s′)\displaystyle{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{issue}}(j,s,s^{\prime}) ⇔s′=s∨s′=s∪{j},𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M(s,s′)⇔s′=s.\displaystyle\iff s^{\prime}=s\ \lor\ s^{\prime}=s\cup\{j\},\qquad{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}_{M}}(s,s^{\prime})\iff s^{\prime}=s.

The module has these two tools. The model of 𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾\mathsf{issue} includes the register before and after the instruction is added, while idle leaves it unchanged. Entries are retained even when a request times out, since an unacknowledged instruction may still produce a charge.

Proposition 2 (Custody).

For the module defined by 25, assume that, in every execution of its tools, including idle,

  1. only 𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾⁡(j)\mathsf{issue}(j) changes the register, by adding jj at most once during the invocation. Entries are never removed or modified;

  2. an instruction is submitted only by 𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾\mathsf{issue} after it is registered. The history JJ retains all submissions, and no other action adds an instruction or changes its terms.

Then 𝖢𝗈𝗏M​(𝖳)\mathsf{Cov}_{M}({\mathsf{T}}) and 𝖥𝗂𝖽M​(𝖳)\mathsf{Fid}_{M}({\mathsf{T}}) hold for 𝖳∈{𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾,𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M}{\mathsf{T}}\in\{\mathsf{issue},\mathsf{idle}_{M}\}.

Proof.

Item H1 limits register changes to those in 25, establishing coverage for both tools. Starting from correspondence, every initial member of JJ remains registered by Item H1. Every new member is registered before submission by Item H2, and its entry is retained. Thus J⁡(w′)J(w^{\prime}) remains contained in s′s^{\prime} throughout either invocation, establishing fidelity. ∎

The access restriction in Item H2 applies complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975) to the authority to issue payment instructions. Keeping the credentials under the Airlock’s control and requiring the provider to accept only authenticated instructions can support this restriction, as in capability-based protection (Dennis and Van Horn, 1966; Miller, 2006). The Airlock’s implementation must protect the register and record each instruction before sending it. The payment provider must preserve its terms and reject submissions made without the required authority. These conditions do not assert that the account balance remains fixed while the module is idle. Charges from earlier instructions may continue, and their bounds require the additional service condition in E.2.

Formal interfaces. A service can specify which responses it may return to a request and how they relate to that request and to its previous interactions. Such a specification gives a module a basis for modelling calls to the service without describing its implementation. The module’s routine records the responses it receives, and its correspondence connects those records to responses actually issued by the service and permitted by its specification.

For example, a booking request can identify a hotel, dates and a maximum price. The specification may allow either a rejection or a confirmation carrying those dates and a price within the requested limit. Concretely, an implementation could maintain a register of response records, stored in memory or in a database. Each record would contain the request, the returned status and, for a confirmation, the booking identifier, dates and price. The routine authenticates the response and adds its record to the register. The module’s state represents the register’s contents as a collection of such records, so the model can express which additions are permitted without committing to a particular storage implementation. Correspondence then relates each record to a response actually issued by the service. Whether the hotel honours the confirmation is a further property, supported by the reservation condition in Example 3.

The same construction applies to any service with a specified request–response interface. Let 𝑅𝑒𝑞\mathit{Req} be the set of requests and 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝\mathit{Resp} the set of response events. An event contains the request, the returned data and any time or historical information used by the specification. Write 𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(e)\mathsf{request}(e) for its request and 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⁡(e)\mathsf{Spec}(e) for the statement that the response is permitted for that request. Take I𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒=𝑅𝑒𝑞I_{\mathsf{query}}=\mathit{Req} and let ΣM\Sigma_{M} consist of finite sets of response events. With H⁡(w)H(w) denoting the history of events actually issued by the service, define

ρM​(w,s)\displaystyle\rho_{M}(w,s) ⇔∀e∈s.e∈H⁡(w)∧𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⁡(e),\displaystyle\iff\forall e\in s.\ e\in H(w)\wedge\mathsf{Spec}(e), (26)
𝖣𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒​(q,s,s′)\displaystyle{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{query}}(q,s,s^{\prime}) ⇔s′=s∨∃e.𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(e)=q∧𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼⁡(e)∧s′=s∪{e},\displaystyle\iff s^{\prime}=s\ \lor\ \exists e.\ \mathsf{request}(e)=q\wedge\mathsf{Spec}(e)\wedge s^{\prime}=s\cup\{e\},
𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M​(s,s′)\displaystyle{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}_{M}}(s,s^{\prime}) ⇔s′=s.\displaystyle\iff s^{\prime}=s.

The model allows any response permitted by the specification, while correspondence requires each recorded response to have actually been issued. The following proposition separates the conditions needed on the service from those needed on the routine that records its responses.

Proposition 3 (Formal interface).

For the module defined by 26, assume that HH retains its events and that, in every execution of its tools, including idle,

  1. every response event issued by the service satisfies 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Spec};

  2. only 𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒⁡(q)\mathsf{query}(q) changes the log. It either leaves it unchanged or appends one event ee issued for qq, after authenticating its origin and recording its contents correctly. Entries are never removed or modified.

Then 𝖢𝗈𝗏M​(𝖳)\mathsf{Cov}_{M}({\mathsf{T}}) and 𝖥𝗂𝖽M​(𝖳)\mathsf{Fid}_{M}({\mathsf{T}}) hold for 𝖳∈{𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗋𝗒,𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾M}{\mathsf{T}}\in\{\mathsf{query},\mathsf{idle}_{M}\}.

Proof.

By Item F2, any change appends one response event for the current request, and Item F1 makes that event satisfy 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Spec}. This proves coverage. Initially valid entries remain in HH, since history is retained. Each new entry is an issued event by Item F2 and satisfies 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Spec} by Item F1, proving fidelity. During idle the log is unchanged and its entries remain valid. ∎

If no response has arrived, or the call times out without recording one, the log remains unchanged, which the model permits. An error returned by the service can instead be a response allowed by 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Spec}. Condition Item F1 requires the actual responses to obey that specification, for example by respecting the requested dates and price limit. This is a property of the service, for which verification or testing can provide evidence (Tretmans, 2008; Bornholt et al., 2021; Disselkoen et al., 2024). Condition Item F2 concerns the Airlock’s routine: it must authenticate the response and record it against the correct request. Authentication establishes who sent the response, but cannot by itself establish that its contents satisfy the specification or that the hotel will honour the booking (Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).

Domain invariants. Interpreting a service’s records often relies on properties of the system in which the service operates. A booking confirmation can stand for a reservation still held only if the hotel maintains that reservation under the agreed conditions. Such properties can support many different contracts using the same service. We express them by a predicate 𝖪\mathsf{K} on worlds, and ask that the module’s routines and the outside interactions that remain possible preserve 𝖪\mathsf{K} whenever it holds initially. This is the sense in which 𝖪\mathsf{K} is a domain invariant. It describes a relationship that the system must maintain, which may involve facts absent from the module’s state.

Consider a module whose state is a measurement π:𝒲M→ΣM\pi:\mathcal{W}_{M}\to\Sigma_{M}, with ΣM=π⁡(𝒲M)\Sigma_{M}=\pi(\mathcal{W}_{M}). Here s=π⁡(w)s=\pi(w) is the current, possibly unobserved state, as in Sec. 3. For example, a module that monitors a mailbox can take π⁡(w)\pi(w) to be its current contents. Write 𝖯𝖾𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗀⁡(w,m)\mathsf{Pending}(w,m) when message mm has been delivered to the mailbox but has not yet been acknowledged by the module’s processing routine, and 𝖠𝗏𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖺𝖻𝗅𝖾⁡(w,m)\mathsf{Available}(w,m) when it can still be retrieved from the mailbox. A retention condition on the mail service is

𝖪(w)⇔∀m.𝖯𝖾𝗇𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗀(w,m)⟹𝖠𝗏𝖺𝗂𝗅𝖺𝖻𝗅𝖾(w,m).\mathsf{K}(w)\quad\iff\quad\forall m.\ \mathsf{Pending}(w,m)\implies\mathsf{Available}(w,m).

This condition allows new messages to arrive and acknowledged messages to be removed, while requiring pending messages to remain available. Delivery and acknowledgement belong to the world’s history, so a correct reading of an empty mailbox alone does not establish that no messages are pending. That conclusion also uses 𝖪\mathsf{K}. The module’s guarantees therefore depend on the routines and mail service preserving this retention condition.

We include both measurement agreement and the domain invariant in the correspondence:

ρM​(w,s)⇔s=π⁡(w)∧𝖪⁡(w).\rho_{M}(w,s)\iff s=\pi(w)\wedge\mathsf{K}(w). (27)

The tools retain their models 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} and their execution effects E𝖳E_{\mathsf{T}} and E^𝖳\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}. Coverage requires Ξ𝖳​(i,s)∧E𝖳​(i,s,s′)⟹𝖣𝖳​(i,s,s′)\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\wedge E_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\implies{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}), as in 19, and must be established for the chosen models. The role of 𝖪\mathsf{K} is to justify the additional relationships asserted by correspondence. To establish fidelity, we check that the actual joint effects E^𝖳\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}} preserve 𝖪\mathsf{K} while the state continues to agree with π\pi. The following proposition expresses these conditions and shows how 𝖪\mathsf{K} can then support an adequacy argument.

Proposition 4 (Domain invariant).

For a module with correspondence given by 27, assume that

  1. in every execution of its tools, including idle, the state at every instant is π\pi of the world at that instant;

  2. for every 𝖳∈𝒯M{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}_{M} and all inputs, worlds and states,

    Ξ𝖳​(i,s)∧𝖪⁡(w)∧E^𝖳​(i,w,s,w′,s′)⟹𝖪⁡(w′).\Xi_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s)\wedge\mathsf{K}(w)\wedge\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime})\implies\mathsf{K}(w^{\prime}).

Then 𝖥𝗂𝖽M​(𝖳)\mathsf{Fid}_{M}({\mathsf{T}}) holds for every 𝖳∈𝒯M{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}_{M}. For predicates 𝖢\mathsf{C} on ΣM\Sigma_{M} and 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} on 𝒲M\mathcal{W}_{M}, adequacy follows if

∀w∈𝒲M𝖪⁡(w)∧𝖢⁡(π⁡(w))⟹𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w).\forall w\in\mathcal{W}_{M}\qquad\mathsf{K}(w)\wedge\mathsf{C}(\pi(w))\implies\mathsf{Safe}(w). (28)
Proof.

Consider an enabled invocation starting from ρM​(w,s)\rho_{M}(w,s) and any joint effect E^𝖳​(i,w,s,w′,s′)\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}). Initial correspondence gives 𝖪⁡(w)\mathsf{K}(w), so Item M2 yields 𝖪⁡(w′)\mathsf{K}(w^{\prime}), while Item M1 gives s′=π⁡(w′)s^{\prime}=\pi(w^{\prime}). Thus ρM​(w′,s′)\rho_{M}(w^{\prime},s^{\prime}) holds, proving fidelity. Finally, correspondence and 𝖢⁡(s)\mathsf{C}(s) imply 𝖪⁡(w)\mathsf{K}(w) and 𝖢⁡(π⁡(w))\mathsf{C}(\pi(w)), so 28 gives 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w)\mathsf{Safe}(w). ∎

Conditions such as Item M2 express what the system relies on about its environment, as domain assumptions do in requirements engineering (Jackson, 1995; Zave and Jackson, 1997). In the mailbox example, Item M2 requires pending messages to remain available throughout processing and waiting. A routine that removes a message must therefore have acknowledged it by the time removal takes effect. Preservation of 𝖪\mathsf{K} can be proved for a specified service whose operations enforce these conditions. Applying that proof to an actual service also requires evidence that its implementation and the permitted outside interactions satisfy the specification (Lee, 2016).

Conditions on outside changes also inform the choice of 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}. For example, a bound on how rapidly a price can change must account for the whole duration of an invocation or idle interval. An unbounded idle period can require a much broader model, and the contract may then be unable to authorize an operation. Such coverage arguments concern the possible effects on the state, alongside the invariant-preservation argument above.

Another example concerns the expert tools introduced in Sec. 3.5.2, such as an LLM asked to assess whether a hotel is suitable. An expert module can describe the history of these assessments, with π\pi extracting the judgment returned by a particular invocation. A state field then denotes that identified assessment, so observing it again retrieves the same result even when the procedure could give a different answer on a new call. The correspondence establishes which procedure produced the judgment. A contract using the module must additionally specify what reliance on that judgment means for its goal or safety property, which is a question of adequacy.

The payment and booking examples of Appendix E combine these constructions. In the ledger, custody supports uj≤rju_{j}\leq r_{j}, while the provider’s charge bound supports aj≤uja_{j}\leq u_{j}. For bookings, recording an authentic confirmation supports the historical claim, while the hotel’s commitment supports the claim that the room remains held. These conditions belong to different parties even when they support one correspondence. Table 2 places these constructions in the broader setting of interactions with the world, from protected records to changing quantities and service responses. It connects what the tools must model, including while idle, to the choices available to a contract and to approaches developed in the literature.

6.4  From local to global guarantees

The preceding constructions identify conditions on routines, records and services that support a module’s guarantees. Once coverage and fidelity have been established for each module, we can combine them for a contract whose state is their product. For a tool that operates on one component, the proof must account for that operation and for the other components while they wait. More generally, the same argument applies to a combined tool when each component’s model and effects cover the whole invocation. A control routine that cannot be decomposed in this way needs a separate argument over the full state.

Theorem 6 (From local to global guarantees).

Let M1,…,MnM_{1},\ldots,M_{n} be capability modules, with n≥1n\geq 1, and let 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} have state space Σ=∏k=1nΣMk\Sigma=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\Sigma_{M_{k}}. Set 𝒲=∏k=1n𝒲Mk\mathcal{W}=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\mathcal{W}_{M_{k}} and ρ⁡(w,s)⇔⋀k=1nρMk​(wk,sk)\rho(w,s)\iff\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}\rho_{M_{k}}(w_{k},s_{k}). Suppose each contract tool, including control, is a tensor of tools from the MkM_{k}, with the conjunction model of 21. Assume the nn-component form of 22 for every such tool. Then

⋀k=1n⋀𝖳∈𝒯Mk𝖢𝗈𝗏Mk​(𝖳)⟹A2,⋀k=1n⋀𝖳∈𝒯Mk𝖥𝗂𝖽Mk​(𝖳)⟹15.\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}\ \bigwedge_{{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}_{M_{k}}}\mathsf{Cov}_{M_{k}}({\mathsf{T}})\implies\text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{ass:transition-coverage}},\qquad\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}\ \bigwedge_{{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}_{M_{k}}}\mathsf{Fid}_{M_{k}}({\mathsf{T}})\implies\text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eq:fidelity}}. (29)
Proof.

An enabled tensor has an enabled component on each module, because a witness to its conjunction model supplies a witness to every component model. By 22, each joint effect projects to an effect of that component. Local coverage therefore gives each conjunct of the tensor model, proving coverage. Local fidelity preserves each conjunct of ρ\rho, which proves 15, the first line of A5. ∎

The result explains what can be reused when a contract combines, for example, payment and booking. The proofs about recording payment instructions and booking responses can be established separately. To use them together, we check that running either routine does not introduce changes excluded by the other module’s effects. Once this compatibility holds, the proofs establish coverage and fidelity for the combined tools, without a new proof for every payment–booking combination. The second line of A5, the start, is a property of the contract’s control step (Sec. 5.1).

The theorem is stated using execution effects EE and E^\widehat{E}. To obtain guarantees independent of the requesting agent, its argument can first be applied to the reference executions of Sec. 5.2, with the same compatibility condition on their effects. Under A7, Lemma 2 transfers the resulting coverage and fidelity to executions with any agent. This identifies the separate roles of composition and isolation: composition combines the component arguments, while isolation makes the resulting argument apply regardless of the agent’s computation and requests.

A contract can also restrict an existing tool by a precondition, as in Sec. 3.5.2. The new model is the conjunction of that precondition with the original model. Whenever it is enabled, the precondition holds and the original tool is enabled, so the original coverage proof also establishes coverage of the restricted model. The routine and correspondence have not changed, so the same fidelity proof applies. The restriction thus changes which calls can be authorized while retaining the established guarantees for those calls.

Checking an extension. We want to reuse the guarantees of an existing module when adding state fields, correspondence claims or routines. To do so, we first establish that the existing routines retain their guarantees in the extended system, then check that they preserve the added correspondence and that the new routines satisfy the requirements on the full state. The completed-purchase register introduced above illustrates why these checks are needed. An existing booking routine leaves this register unchanged, but that alone does not establish the added correspondence ρ′\rho^{\prime}. If an entry means that a confirmation was issued, later cancellation need not invalidate it. If it means that the booking is still held, cancellation can make it false even though the entry has not changed.

More precisely, the effects of each existing routine, projected onto 𝒲M\mathcal{W}_{M} and ΣM\Sigma_{M}, must remain within its original effects, and ZZ must remain unchanged. Their coverage proofs then establish the lifted models in 24, and their fidelity proofs preserve ρM\rho_{M}. For each such tool, including idle, we additionally check that an enabled invocation starting from ρM∧ρ′\rho_{M}\wedge\rho^{\prime} preserves ρ′\rho^{\prime}. For an added routine, such as the purchase routine, coverage must hold on the full state ΣM×Z\Sigma_{M}\times Z and fidelity must preserve both correspondences. An added control routine must also satisfy A3 for the chosen contract clause. These checks allow an extension to reuse the original proofs while establishing the additional claims it makes.

The conditions used in these proofs provide a way to organize the argument for the complete contract. Write LkL_{k} for the supporting conditions of module MkM_{k}, such as the register and issuance requirements Item H1–Item H2 for payments or the response and recording requirements Item F1–Item F2 for bookings. Suppose they establish its local guarantees for reference executions, and check compatibility in 22 for those same effects. Under the remaining construction hypotheses of Thm. 6, composition followed by isolation gives

L1∧⋯∧Ln∧A7∧compatibility of reference effects⟹A2∧15.L_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge L_{n}\ \wedge\ \text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{ass:isolation}}\ \wedge\ \text{compatibility of reference effects}\ \implies\ \text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{ass:transition-coverage}}\wedge\text{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eq:fidelity}}. (30)

Figure 7 illustrates how this argument can be repeated within a module. The contract environment is the product M1⊗M2⊗M5M_{1}\otimes M_{2}\otimes M_{5}, where M5=ext⁡(M3⊗M4)M_{5}=\operatorname{ext}(M_{3}\otimes M_{4}). In the figure, 𝖢𝗈𝗏N\mathsf{Cov}_{N} and 𝖥𝗂𝖽N\mathsf{Fid}_{N} abbreviate the coverage and fidelity requirements for every tool of a module NN, including idle, for reference executions. We first combine the guarantees of M3M_{3} and M4M_{4}, then check the additions that produce M5M_{5}. Once these checks are complete, M5M_{5} supplies guarantees in the same form as the other modules and can be used in the outer product. Each product step requires the hypotheses of Thm. 6, and A7 transfers the resulting guarantees to every agent.

The colours illustrate one possible assessment of the conditions supporting this construction. They apply separately to coverage and fidelity, while the module boxes remain white. The internal claims are proved from their dependencies, while the leaf claims identify where responsibility is assigned, risk is mitigated or risk is accepted. Coverage and fidelity of the same module may therefore receive different treatments. These tags describe how a condition is handled, and a different use of the same module may require a different assignment. In Sec. 6.5 we explain how to organize such an assessment as an assurance case, connecting the mathematical argument to evidence and responsibilities.

Reusing module arguments reduces repeated verification, although compatibility and extension checks still depend on the combination. It also helps assess a change: if a payment provider changes its access policy, we can follow the branches from that condition to the contracts whose proofs use it. The tree identifies the affected arguments. Whether the resulting system failure can also affect other modules depends on their interactions, particularly on whether compatibility still holds.

Adequacy. The theorem establishes coverage and fidelity. The implication ρ⁡(w,s)∧𝖢⁡(s)⟹𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w)\rho(w,s)\wedge\mathsf{C}(s)\implies\mathsf{Safe}(w) in A6 still concerns the contract as a whole. Its correspondences may be local while its protection involves several resources. With two payment providers under one budget, for instance, a1​(w)≤b1​(s)a^{1}(w)\leq b^{1}(s) and a2​(w)≤b2​(s)a^{2}(w)\leq b^{2}(s), together with b1​(s)+b2​(s)≤Bb^{1}(s)+b^{2}(s)\leq B, entail a1​(w)+a2​(w)≤Ba^{1}(w)+a^{2}(w)\leq B. The parties must also validate that this formal protection is the one they intend. The same distinction applies to the goal and 18.

Beyond products. This construction uses disjoint coordinates for the resources and their states. More general forms of composition can support shared resources or guarantees between interacting components. Separation logic and resource algebras provide ways to describe shared resources with separated permissions (O’Hearn et al., 2001; Reynolds, 2002; Jung et al., 2015). Interface theories and assume–guarantee contracts organize interactions through specified interfaces (de Alfaro and Henzinger, 2001; Benveniste et al., 2018), while layered verification establishes a component against the specification of the layer below (Gu et al., 2015). These approaches could support further capability constructions. Here the product and extension identify the proof obligations for the cases developed above.

6.5  From assumptions to responsibilities

The preceding constructions allow a contract to reuse its modules’ guarantees. To apply them, we need to identify how their supporting conditions are met by the routines and services involved. For a payment module, this includes how instructions are recorded, who holds the credentials and which submissions the provider accepts. Following these dependencies identifies what to check and who can supply the evidence. Organizing the argument in this way produces an assurance case: a structured argument explaining why a system should satisfy a specified property, supported by evidence for the conditions on which it relies (Kelly and Weaver, 2004; Bloomfield and Rushby, 2020).

Figure 8 organizes this assessment for the complete contract. Its first level gives the six assumptions of Thm. 3, with their requirements and the parties expected to support them. The module arguments of Fig. 7 establish coverage and fidelity, while the other branches concern the checker, initialization and control, execution, and adequacy. Isolation connects these arguments to arbitrary agents: by Lemma 2, the reference-execution guarantees apply regardless of the agent’s computation and requests. The Airlock’s provider establishes this restriction on access, as described in Sec. 5.2.

The colours distinguish how the parties propose to support a condition or address the possibility that it fails:

  • •

    Proof. A mathematical argument establishes a property from specified premises. For example, the routine can be proved to register each instruction before submitting it. Its assumptions about storage and execution remain explicit dependencies.

  • •

    Assigned responsibility. A named party commits to maintaining a condition, such as restricting use of the payment credentials or honouring a reservation. The tree records who must support that commitment with evidence and who is responsible for failures.

  • •

    Mitigation. Measures such as testing, independent checks or monitoring reduce the risk of a failure or its consequences. For a service response, this could include checking its fields against the request before recording it. The remaining uncertainty must still be assessed.

  • •

    Accepted risk. The parties identify a possibility of failure or a gap in the protection and agree to proceed despite it. For a theorem’s premise, this records the limit of their confidence that it holds. For the scope of 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe}, it records the risk that the specified protection does not cover everything they intended.

The four tags retain these meanings throughout the assessment, while their placement in Figs. 7 and 8 illustrates possible choices. They may coexist, for example when a service provider accepts responsibility for a condition while monitoring supplies further evidence about whether it holds. In Fig. 8, fidelity is green because it is derived from the conditions below it. The grey box under adequacy records a different decision: the parties accept that the scope of protection expressed by 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} may be incomplete, even when the adequacy implication itself has been proved. The white annotation about the meaning of fields identifies a specification choice.

The expanded part follows fidelity, whose supporting conditions often involve several parties. It groups them by the questions to address when interpreting and maintaining the correspondence. The labels Item H1–Item H2, Item F1–Item F2 and Item M1–Item M2 connect these branches to the conditions in the preceding propositions. A module may combine several of these arguments.

Custody. We ask who can change the protected records and authorize the operations they describe. In the payment module, the routine registers each instruction before submission, and the provider accepts submissions only through the protected authority. Conditions Item H1–Item H2 express these requirements. Proposition 2 shows that they establish coverage and fidelity. Their justification combines an argument about the routine with evidence about access permissions and the provider’s acceptance of instructions.

Formal interfaces. When a module records a service’s response, we need to know what the service may report and how the routine receives and records it. Conditions Item F1–Item F2 separate these questions. A booking service must return permitted responses, and the receiving routine must authenticate them and associate them with the correct requests. Proposition 3 then establishes coverage and fidelity. The service provider supports the first condition, while the receiving routine’s implementer and operator support the second.

External behaviour. Some claims require a service to maintain a condition after replying, or while the module waits. A hotel must retain an unexpired reservation, and a mail service may be required to retain unacknowledged messages. The predicate 𝖪\mathsf{K} of Prop. 4 expresses such domain invariants. Its preservation, together with agreement between the state and its measurement, establishes fidelity. Coverage also requires an account of possible state changes. These arguments may rely on service commitments, verified rules or bounds on outside interactions, as illustrated in Tab. 2.

Agreed meaning. Before checking whether a field describes the world correctly, we must specify what it describes. A booking field may record that a confirmation was issued or assert that a room is still held. These choices require different correspondences. In the measurement construction, choosing π\pi specifies the reading, while Item M1 requires the state to agree with it. For an expert tool, the record can identify the procedure and invocation that produced a judgment. The parties decide what reliance on that judgment means for the protection or goal, connecting correspondence to adequacy and to 18.

For a payment module, the resulting assurance case can connect its coverage and fidelity proofs to a checked implementation, an assessment of access permissions and evidence about the provider’s acceptance of instructions. The tree records how these pieces support the overall guarantee and makes any unsupported conditions visible. The propositions supply the mathematical implications, while the evidence supports applying their premises to the routines and services that will actually be used (Hawkins et al., 2011). This includes specifications and interactions with external components, which are known sources of failures even in verified systems (Fonseca et al., 2017).

The work can be reused along with the module: a new contract checks that its supporting conditions still apply and that the composition and any extensions meet the requirements of Sec. 6.4. It then uses the existing proofs and evidence while supplying its own clause, control and adequacy arguments. If a payment provider changes its access policy, the dependencies identify which custody arguments and contracts need review. In Sec. 8.3 we discuss recording these responsibilities and agreeing on responses to failures. The same assessment supports completion, where the correspondence must justify the world goal when settlement begins.

7  Mechanization

We provide a Lean 4 mechanization of PC2 (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021), available in the GitHub repository. The repository contains the formal definitions and checked proofs, identifies the corresponding results in this paper and makes their assumptions explicit. It also documents the implementation and provides instructions for reproducing the checks.

8  Practical use and remaining risks

The preceding sections establish how PC2 can enforce a contract and how its guarantees depend on the routines, services and host that support execution. Using such a contract also requires the parties to understand what they are agreeing to, the agent to find proofs at an acceptable cost, and arrangements for the risks that remain assumed. These questions connect the construction to work on specification, automated reasoning and cooperation between parties with different interests. We discuss possible ways to address them, and what would need to be evaluated. Developing and validating these arrangements is outside the scope of the present work.

8.1  Writing and understanding agreements

An enforceable agreement need not be the agreement its parties intended. A travel contract might require a flight and a hotel without requiring their dates and destinations to match. Every accepted call could then satisfy the clauses while the resulting trip is unusable. The mathematical adequacy condition in A6 connects 𝖢\mathsf{C} to a specified 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe}, but deciding whether 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} captures the intended protection remains a separate task. This is closely related to the difficulties of specifying objectives for optimizing systems and of writing complete agreements (Manheim and Garrabrant, 2018; Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield, 2019).

A possible response is to assist the parties with formalizer agents, building on work on autoformalization (Wu et al., 2022). A formalizer would draft clauses from the parties’ intentions, explain the resulting clauses in ordinary language, and search for compliant states that expose an unintended interpretation. For the travel example, it could present a trip whose bookings satisfy the individual requirements but cannot be used together. These examples give the parties concrete questions to resolve before signing. Capability modules and previously reviewed contract templates can also reduce the amount of specification that must be written afresh. Once ρ\rho, 𝖢\mathsf{C} and 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe} have been specified, formal reasoning can establish their mathematical relationship. Reviewing the explanations and counterexamples serves the different purpose of checking that these are the relationships the parties want.

Expert judgments. Some requirements, such as whether a hotel suits a client’s description, depend on the experts introduced in Sec. 3.5.2. A fixed expert procedure gives these requirements an agreed interpretation, but its judgments may be influenced by how evidence is presented. A hotel description could be written to obtain a favourable assessment without corresponding to a desirable hotel. The parties can test proposed experts on borderline and adversarial examples, specify which evidence they receive, and limit repeated attempts to obtain a favourable verdict. When an assessment is intended to remain binding, the contract can retain it and specify when new evidence permits reconsideration. These choices make the decision procedure more predictable and harder to manipulate. Their effectiveness, and whether the procedure captures the intended judgment, require evaluation beyond checking the proofs that use its answers.

Negotiation. The same review matters when an agreement is negotiated. A party may propose clauses that are formally consistent but unexpectedly favourable to itself, so the final agreement must be assessed as a whole. Choreographic and negotiation languages (Gopinathan et al., 2026; Wyse et al., 2026) provide ways to organize how agents reach agreements. Connecting them to PC2 would require their outputs to determine the clauses, tools and other components of the contract that will actually be enforced. Formalizers could support this process by explaining how a proposed revision changes the permitted outcomes.

8.2  Finding proofs and using contracts in practice

A request without an accepted proof cannot execute, so the ability to find proofs determines whether the agent can carry out its task. Control can still enforce stopping and refund conditions under the timing assumptions of Sec. 5.3. There is no general procedure that decides all obligations expressible in the underlying logic, and proofs that exist may still be difficult to find before their control window expires. The benefit of the construction is that it requires proofs about proposed calls and the tool models, without requiring a proof of the agent’s reasoning or its entire future behaviour. An individual obligation can nevertheless involve substantial reasoning about hidden state and possible outcomes.

Capability modules offer a way to reduce this work. A module can provide lemmas about the effects of its tools, which can be reused across calls and contracts. Common contract templates could then reduce many requests to familiar arithmetic or finite checks, while retaining the possibility of more general clauses. For example, a lemma about a payment routine’s maximum charge can be reused when proving that a particular request preserves a budget. A prover can combine such lemmas with Lean’s tactics and learned proof search (Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). It can run as an assistant to the acting agent, since the correctness guarantee depends on checking the resulting proof rather than on which system produced it. The choice of control window also matters: a proof that tolerates several control steps may remain usable despite the time required to construct and check it.

Confidentiality during inference. Access restrictions must also account for how the agent is run. If it sends its observations to an external inference service, that service receives the information in those requests even when every tool call is proof-gated. The parties therefore need to decide whether the provider is an intended recipient. Where it is not, possible arrangements include inference on a machine under the required access controls or within a confidential computing environment (Chrapek et al., 2025). The permitted recipients and the protections offered by the chosen arrangement must agree with the confidentiality requirements of the contract.

Evaluation. An evaluation of practical use should measure whether contracts capture the intended task, whether the required proofs can be found in time, and whether the resulting system completes useful work at an acceptable total cost. The first question calls for adversarial examples that separate intended outcomes from formally compliant ones. The second calls for measurements of proof-search and checking time, reuse of module lemmas, and requests that expire before authorization. The third includes the cost of constructing the contract, operating control and using external services, compared with other safeguards on the same tasks. Successful task completion must be reported alongside violations and rejected calls, so that rejecting everything cannot count as a successful defense. Such an evaluation would test the proposed use of formalizers and provers, rather than infer their effectiveness from the safety theorem.

8.3  Responsibility and consequences
