The assurance analysis of Sec. 6.5 identifies what supports a guarantee and what remains assumed. The parties must also decide how to proceed with those assumptions. Before signing, they can record each premise that remains, who accepts responsibility for it, the evidence available, and the response agreed for a failure. For the payment ledger of Appendix E, this includes the reservation discipline of the implementation and the charge limits enforced by the payment service. An agreement to answer for a service failure gives the parties a basis for allocating its consequences. It does not replace the evidence that the service respects its limits.

Where failures can be established from records, a contract could include a remedy with a decidable trigger and an available execution routine. Reconciliation of payment instructions against service statements might, for instance, trigger a refund from reserved funds. Deposits or insurance could provide other ways to allocate losses, depending on what events they cover, what evidence establishes a claim, and whether the promised compensation is available. Designing these arrangements is a further question beyond the enforcement mechanism studied here. An automatic remedy itself needs the same coverage, fidelity and adequacy analysis as any other tool. Compensation addresses a consequence of failure, while the safety theorem concerns whether the failure can occur at all. If the available observations cannot distinguish a failure, its resolution requires additional evidence or a risk the parties explicitly accept.

Consequences for others. An agreement may serve its parties while harming others. Credible commitments can sustain harmful coordination or make threats more credible (Hammond et al., 2025). Access to an Airlock could therefore require additional approval or disclosure for certain contracts, alongside restrictions on the resources and operations it provides. These measures raise questions about authority, confidentiality and protection of people outside the agreement. PC2 can enforce agreed requirements, but deciding which agreements should be permitted requires a broader institutional account.

Participation and economic agency. Enforceable commitments could allow people and smaller organizations to delegate to providers whose systems they cannot inspect, while retaining specified limits on the authority they grant. Whether that possibility translates into broad participation also depends on the cost of writing contracts and finding proofs, access to suitable capability modules, and the terms on which Airlock providers offer their services. These questions connect to economic agency and the distribution of AI’s gains (Jacobs and Imas, 2026), and to arguments that access must be accompanied by the infrastructure needed to benefit from AI (Gabriel and Kasirzadeh, 2026). Reusable modules and reviewed templates could lower some of these costs. Fair terms and protection for people outside an agreement require additional institutional arrangements.

9  Related work

PC2 brings together three lines of work: restrictions on what an agent can execute, proofs supplied by an untrusted requester, and arguments connecting a formal specification to the system in which it is used. Table 3 summarizes the enforcement mechanisms. We first explain how proof-carrying changes the task of establishing safety, then compare recent safeguards for agents and the verification, specification and cooperation literature on which the construction builds.

From safety constraints to call obligations. To use an authorization policy for state safety, its author must establish that every permitted call preserves the intended constraint. As tools interact with hidden information, external services and changing state, this can require substantial reasoning about all the situations in which the policy allows execution. A policy can be too restrictive, excluding safe calls, or leave safety gaps despite being enforced correctly.

In PC2, the author specifies what must remain true of the state, through 𝖢\mathsf{C}, together with models 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} of the tools’ possible effects. These determine the obligation for each requested call, accounting for hidden state and intervening control steps (Def. 3 and 4). The agent must prove this obligation for the call it has chosen. No separate permission policy needs to be designed and proved to preserve 𝖢\mathsf{C} for every call it permits. Each call’s proof establishes enabledness and preservation at all compliant active states compatible with the view and all active states admitted by the control window, covering every outcome allowed by the tool model. From these individual justifications and automatic control, Thm. 1 establishes compliance throughout execution once the contract has started. The agent can change its strategy without needing to verify that strategy. Coverage, fidelity and adequacy connect the argument to the executing routines and world safety (Sec. 4 and 5).

Producing proofs and checking them. The distinction between finding a proof and checking one underlies proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997). Finding an argument may require substantial search, auxiliary lemmas and problem-specific reasoning. A supplied proof records the steps that justify the conclusion, allowing a checker to verify them against the logical rules without discovering the argument itself. In PC2, this places the work of justifying a call with the agent requesting it, while the Airlock checks the result. Enforcement therefore does not require a general algorithm that decides whether each obligation is true. Constraints and tool models can give rise to undecidable obligations without preventing the Airlock from checking proofs of particular instances.

This separation allows the reasoning used to justify calls to become more sophisticated without changing the criterion for accepting them. Routine obligations can use existing automation and reusable lemmas, while more difficult ones can require additional search or specialist provers (Sec. 8.2). An accepted proof establishes the required preservation condition regardless of how it was found. If the agent cannot supply one, the requested call does not execute. Task completion may then fail, while checked calls and automatic control continue to provide the safety guarantee under the stated assumptions.

Defenses for tool-using agents. Prompt injection (Perez and Ribeiro, 2022; Greshake et al., 2023) allows content encountered during a task to steer an agent away from its instructions. AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) provides an environment for evaluating such attacks and their defenses on realistic tasks. Deterministic defenses instead restrict execution independently of whether the model follows its instructions. CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025) separates privileged planning from untrusted data and enforces capabilities on tool use. Progent (Shi et al., 2025) enforces programmable privilege policies, while FIDES (Costa et al., 2025) and RTBAS (Zhong et al., 2025) use information-flow restrictions. PC2 shares the principle that an adversarial model must remain subject to the execution mechanism. Its obligations address what the permitted call can do: the proof must cover every modelled outcome from the compliant active states compatible with the published view, including the changes allowed before execution.

Formal policies and contracts for agents. FORGE (Palumbo et al., 2026) enforces Datalog authorization rules over execution histories and externally supplied facts. Its enforcement argument relies on complete mediation and faithful policy-relevant observations. The guarantee concerns enforcement of the supplied policy, leaving its relationship to state safety to a separate argument.

Alignment Contracts (David et al., 2026) give a decidable contract language for permitted effects, budgets and disclosures. Their mechanized soundness theorem establishes that the event trace produced by a monitor satisfies the contract, independently of the agent’s policy. Applying the theorem requires correct event extraction and complete mediation, which the work explicitly distinguishes from its mechanized results. It also separates formal enforcement from heuristic mitigation of attacks involving the contents of permitted messages. The guarantee concerns the events represented in the contract language, with unmodelled disclosures and payload semantics outside its scope.

When authorization rules are supplied separately from a desired state constraint, their author must establish that every permitted call preserves that constraint. A policy can be too restrictive, rejecting safe calls, or insufficiently restrictive, allowing violations despite being enforced correctly. PC2 asks the contract author to specify what must remain true of the state, through 𝖢\mathsf{C}, together with models of the tools’ possible effects. From these objects, the published view and the allowed control steps, it derives the obligation for each requested call (Def. 3 and 4). The proof must establish enabledness and preservation of 𝖢\mathsf{C} at every compliant active state compatible with the view and every active state admitted by its control window. The agent can therefore choose any strategy for carrying out the task, provided its calls carry proofs of these obligations. No separate permission policy needs to be designed and justified: each accepted proof establishes the preservation condition itself. This condition is exact relative to the chosen models and the states admitted by the view and control window: every rule that safely admits calls on the basis of the view implies it (Proposition A.1). Conservative models and difficulties in finding proofs can still prevent safe calls from executing (Sec. 4.1 and 8.2).

Proof-carrying provides a further form of generality. The Airlock checks a supplied proof of the constructed obligation, so its enforcement does not require a decision procedure for the obligation itself. The contract’s constraints and tool models can therefore give rise to undecidable obligations while retaining an independently checkable justification for every authorized call. Under the assumptions of Thm. 1, these checks and the automatic control steps preserve 𝖢\mathsf{C} throughout execution once the contract has started. Fidelity and adequacy connect this execution guarantee to world safety in Sec. 5, and Sec. 6.1 and 6.5 develop reusable module guarantees and the evidence and responsibilities supporting their application. Goal-gated settlement further allows parties to agree on a completion procedure whose authorized execution requires no subsequent client approval.

Proofs, evidence and resource contracts. Type-Checked Compliance (Rashie and Rashi, 2026) proposes translating financial policies into Lean and checking proposed actions before invoking an API. Like PC2, it places a formal check between the proposed action and its execution. It does not develop the transition-based argument relating accepted obligations to all possible intermediate states and then to safety in the world. Proof-Carrying Agent Actions (Wang, 2026) uses “proof” for structured evidence attached to an action, including approval receipts, recorded assumptions and material for replay. Such evidence supports accountability, but is different from a checked derivation of an obligation over possible tool outcomes.

Agent Behavioral Contracts (Bhardwaj, 2026) develops a probabilistic account of compliance, drift and recovery, with composition results under assumptions on these processes. Resource-bounded Agent Contracts (Ye and Tan, 2026) organizes budgets, deadlines and delegation, and explicitly distinguishes stopping future calls from preventing an overrun within a call. PC2’s execution guarantee includes the states reached within each call and during control, rather than only the conditions checked when a new call is requested. Under its stated assumptions, preservation of the contract holds at every instant for arbitrary requests and proposed proofs.

Runtime enforcement and shields. Execution monitoring studies which properties can be enforced by observing a program and stopping unacceptable behaviour. Schneider’s characterization (Schneider, 2000) identifies safety as necessary for this form of enforcement: violations must be witnessed by an execution prefix. Shield synthesis (Bloem et al., 2015) and shielded reinforcement learning (Alshiekh et al., 2018) construct a component that prevents unsafe actions independently of the agent’s policy. Shielding has also been developed for continuous state and action spaces (Kim et al., 2024). In PC2, the Airlock checks a supplied proof rather than deciding the truth of the obligation by a general safety-analysis procedure. This permits predicates and state spaces beyond those supported by a particular synthesis algorithm. Relative to the chosen tool models, the obligation asks exactly for admissibility throughout the control window of every compliant active state with the published view: like the maximally permissive supervisor of supervisory control (Ramadge and Wonham, 1987), it restricts the agent only where the contract requires (Proposition A.1). It imposes no further restriction on how the agent chooses its actions or constructs its proof. Obtaining that proof is the task discussed in Sec. 8.2.

Proof-carrying code and authentication. Proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997) places proof construction with an untrusted code producer and proof checking with the consumer. Proof-carrying authentication (Appel and Felten, 1999) applies the same division to requests for access under a logical policy. PC2 adopts this established separation of responsibilities for tool calls. Its certificate concerns the effects of a particular requested operation, including nondeterministic outcomes and facts hidden by the view, while delayed obligations keep the certificate applicable as control runs. This makes the proof gate part of a continuing interaction with a changing system. The acting model and the prover can be replaced without changing the logical criterion for accepting a request.

Reasoning transparency. Inspecting an agent’s reasoning can help identify deception and unexpected behaviour, but the usefulness of this evidence depends on how much of the reasoning is visible and faithfully reported (Shah and Dragan, 2026). PC2 asks for a different kind of evidence: a proof that the requested call satisfies its obligation. That proof need not describe how the agent chose the call, and it can be produced by a separate prover. Its validity therefore does not depend on the transparency of the acting model. Monitoring can still help identify risks or omissions in the contract, while enforcement of its formal constraints rests on the proof and execution assumptions.

From verification to world safety. A proof about a mathematical description must be connected to the routines and services that execute it. Refinement mappings (Abadi and Lamport, 1991) provide a foundation for relating descriptions at different levels of abstraction. Verification-guided development and differential testing, as used for Cedar (Disselkoen et al., 2024), can establish properties of a model and test whether an implementation agrees with it. Smith (Smith, 1985) examines the role of these interpretations in claims about real systems, and empirical studies of verified systems locate failures in specifications and interactions with unverified components (Fonseca et al., 2017). PC2 makes the relevant connections explicit through coverage, fidelity and adequacy. This separates the proof that execution preserves 𝖢\mathsf{C} from the evidence that compliant states describe safe situations in the world.

The structure follows the satisfaction argument of requirements engineering: properties of the environment together with a system specification must imply the intended requirement (Zave and Jackson, 1997). Assume–guarantee contracts (Benveniste et al., 2018) explain how a component’s guarantees depend on its environment and can support composition. In PC2, capability modules organize such reusable guarantees around tool models and the correspondence between states and the world. Assurance cases then organize the claims and evidence supporting an application of the theorem. They distinguish the argument for safety from confidence in its premises (Hawkins et al., 2011), and examine objections that could defeat that argument (Bloomfield and Rushby, 2020). Section 6.5 uses this perspective to make the dependencies of PC2’s guarantees visible, before Sec. 8.3 considers responsibility for what remains assumed.

Measurements and agreed meaning. Blockchain oracles face a related problem when external facts are used by an executable contract (Eskandari et al., 2021). Attestation and authenticated access can establish the source and processing of data (Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020), while its interpretation still depends on what that source represents. Similarly, the Airlock’s record of an expert verdict establishes which procedure supplied an answer, without by itself establishing the answer’s accuracy. Goodhart’s law (Manheim and Garrabrant, 2018) and incomplete-contract accounts of AI alignment (Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield, 2019) explain why an optimized measure or a formal agreement may miss the intended objective. These concerns do not preclude proving adequacy for specified ρ\rho and 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾\mathsf{Safe}. They motivate examining whether those choices express the intended protection. The distinction between engineering a system to satisfy a model and assessing a model against an existing system (Lee, 2016) also informs the different conditions attached to custody, formal interfaces and external behaviour in Sec. 6.1.

Guaranteed safe AI. The guaranteed safe AI framework (Dalrymple et al., 2024) combines a world model, a safety specification and a verifier. PC2 develops this approach for interactions mediated by tools: tool relations describe the relevant possible changes, the contract specifies constraints, and proofs are checked before requested operations run. The formalization can concentrate on the quantities needed by the contract and can use guarantees supplied by capability modules. It does not require a model of the agent’s internal reasoning. The coverage and fidelity assumptions nevertheless include every relevant change during execution, including outside changes, which is why restricting access and specifying external behaviour matter.

Agents, code and theorem proving. ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) and Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) develop agents that combine reasoning with tool use, while CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024) uses code as the action interface. PC2 retains the ability to choose actions and adapt to observations, adding an obligation to requests that affect the protected system. LeanDojo (Yang et al., 2023), learned provers (Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025) and autoformalization (Wu et al., 2022) supply relevant methods for constructing proofs and specifications. Their application to the obligations and agreements considered here is the practical question developed in Sec. 8.

Commitment and cooperation. Program equilibrium (Tennenholtz, 2004) studies how commitments expressed through programs can support cooperation. PC2 provides a mechanism for enforcing agreed constraints on an agent’s interactions and for invoking authorized settlement without a further client veto. This addresses one part of the principal–agent problem (Jensen and Meckling, 1976), in which a principal delegates work without being able to rely on the delegate’s incentives. It also connects to the risks and opportunities of agents acting for different principals (Hammond et al., 2025). Choreographic and negotiation languages (Gopinathan et al., 2026; Wyse et al., 2026) study how interactions and agreements are organized. PC2 concerns their subsequent enforcement, provided the agreement has been expressed as a contract with the required guarantees.

Confidential computing. Confidential virtual machines, including AMD SEV-SNP (Advanced Micro Devices, 2020), provide mechanisms for protecting execution and attesting a running configuration to other parties. Work on confidential LLM inference (Chrapek et al., 2025) studies their use and cost for the models involved. These mechanisms can support the Airlock’s host and custody requirements and allow parties to identify the code to which they entrust an agreement. Their concrete configuration must provide the isolation and other execution properties identified in Sec. 5.2 and 5.3.

10  Conclusion

PC2 binds an AI agent to a contract it cannot break. The agent keeps its usual loop, and each of its tool calls carries a proof, checked before the call runs. Under the stated assumptions, from the moment the contract starts, the clauses hold at every instant for arbitrary requests and proposed proofs (Thm. 1). Since the Airlock isolates the agent, none of these assumptions depends on it: the checker, the Airlock, the contract and the tools are assessed once, and the guarantees hold for every agent, adversarial or not (Thm. 5). For the standard contract, settlement requires proof of the goal, an authorized settlement request requires no further client approval, and the contract otherwise ends as agreed (Thm. 2). What remains is named. Whether the guarantees reach the world depends on the fidelity of the tools and on the adequacy of the contract, for which we identify concrete deployment conditions (Sec. 5 and 6) and discuss responsibility for remaining assumptions (Sec. 8.3). Whether PC2 is useful depends on whether contracts can be written and proofs found at acceptable cost, which formalizer and prover agents address and a benchmark can measure (Sec. 8). PC2 guarantees safety under its assumptions, and termination by a deadline that the contract states as a clause is part of it (Thm. 5). Other forms of progress, such as settlement once the goal is reached, require additional conditions (Sec. 5.3). This paper treats one acting agent; several agents acting on shared resources, and subcontracts whose obligations survive at any depth, are the subject of a second paper.

Appendices

The appendices provide implementation details, worked examples and further developments of the construction. They can be read independently alongside the relevant sections of the main text.

  • A

    The obligation as a weakest precondition. Why the obligation asks for exactly the safety of a call, and what this means for policy engines.

  • B

    Proof checking. The auxiliary program that checks requests and makes an accepted proof available for one tool invocation.

  • C

    Control design. A construction that maintains compliance by idling, correcting the state or terminating the contract, illustrated with a compute budget.

  • D

    Time between operations. How bounded gaps can be included in the operation models, with a corresponding convention for recorded observations.

  • E

    Correspondence in practice. Payment and booking examples show how state records support guarantees about safety and completion in the world.

  • F

    Failure without isolation. The ways in which actions outside the proof gate can invalidate coverage, fidelity or adequacy.

  • G

    A formal account of isolation. Conditions on concurrent steps and a proof that the agent introduces no effects beyond reference executions.

Appendix A The obligation as a weakest precondition

Weakest preconditions

For a relation RR on states and a predicate QQ, we use the following relational weakest precondition, which requires RR to admit some outcome and all its outcomes to satisfy QQ (Dijkstra, 1975):

wp(R,Q)(s):⇔(∃s′.R(s,s′))∧(∀s′.R(s,s′)⟹Q(s′)).\mathrm{wp}(R,Q)(s)\;:\iff\;\bigl(\exists s^{\prime}.\ R(s,s^{\prime})\bigr)\wedge\bigl(\forall s^{\prime}.\ R(s,s^{\prime})\implies Q(s^{\prime})\bigr).

The outcome is chosen against the requester, and the first conjunct excludes miracles: a relation with no outcome would otherwise establish any QQ. Admissibility is a weakest precondition, 𝒜𝖳​(i,⋅)=wp⁡(𝖣𝖳​(i,⋅,⋅),𝖢)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,\cdot)=\mathrm{wp}({\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,\cdot,\cdot),\mathsf{C}). Here an outcome of 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} is a state admitted during an invocation, rather than necessarily a state at which it returns. The existential condition therefore establishes enabledness in the model, not termination of exec𝖳\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}, and the universal condition requires 𝖢\mathsf{C} throughout the call when coverage holds. In proof-carrying code, the producer proves a verification condition computed as the weakest precondition of its program for the consumer’s safety policy (Necula, 1997); in PC2, the agent proves that of one call.

What the agent knows

The agent does not know the state, only the view vv on which its request is based, the contract, and that the state complies with it, which Thm. 1 makes true. For a call that may start after up to nn control steps, the states it cannot rule out are

Kn(v):={s′∈Σact:∃s∈Σact.𝖵𝗂𝖾𝗐(s)=v∧𝖢(s)∧𝖣ctrl⩽n(s,s′)},K_{n}(v)\;:=\;\bigl\{\,s^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}\;:\;\exists s\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}.\ {\mathsf{View}}(s)=v\wedge\mathsf{C}(s)\wedge{\mathsf{D}}^{\leqslant n}_{\texttt{ctrl}}(s,s^{\prime})\,\bigr\},

and, by Def. 4,

Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v)⇔∀s′∈Kn​(v).wp⁡(𝖣𝖳​(i,⋅,⋅),𝖢)​(s′).\mathrm{Obl}^{\leqslant n}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,v)\iff\forall s^{\prime}\in K_{n}(v).\ \mathrm{wp}\bigl({\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,\cdot,\cdot),\mathsf{C}\bigr)(s^{\prime}). (A.1)

The obligation states that the agent knows the call to be admissible, in the sense of the logic of knowledge, where a fact is known when it holds at every state considered possible (Fagin et al., 1995).

The most permissive gate

A gate specifies, from a request and the view vv on which it is based, whether the call may run: it is a predicate G⁡(𝖳,i,n,v)G({\mathsf{T}},i,n,v). A gate is safe if every call it admits is admissible at every state from which it may start: G⁡(𝖳,i,n,v)G({\mathsf{T}},i,n,v) implies 𝒜𝖳​(i,s′)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s^{\prime}) for every s′∈Kn​(v)s^{\prime}\in K_{n}(v).

Proposition A.1 (The most permissive safe gate).

The obligation is a safe gate, and every safe gate GG satisfies G⁡(𝖳,i,n,v)⟹Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v)G({\mathsf{T}},i,n,v)\implies\mathrm{Obl}^{\leqslant n}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,v) for all 𝖳{\mathsf{T}}, ii, nn and vv. In particular, if the obligations of a contract form an undecidable predicate, every decidable safe gate rejects some call whose obligation holds.

Proof.

By A.1, Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v)\mathrm{Obl}^{\leqslant n}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,v) holds exactly when 𝒜𝖳​(i,s′)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s^{\prime}) holds for every s′∈Kn​(v)s^{\prime}\in K_{n}(v). This is what safety of the obligation requires, and what safety of GG yields when G⁡(𝖳,i,n,v)G({\mathsf{T}},i,n,v) holds. A decidable safe gate that admitted every call whose obligation holds would coincide with the obligation, which would then be decidable. ∎

The proposition is relative to the models and to the view: models that admit fewer outcomes while remaining enabled, views that show more and shorter windows all weaken the obligation, and a gate that also used earlier views could admit more calls, which a contract obtains by putting the relevant history in the state. It concerns one call, while the contract must hold for the rest of the execution. The two agree because the control step keeps 𝖢\mathsf{C} from every compliant active state (A3): a call that keeps 𝖢\mathsf{C} leaves a state from which the contract can be kept, so a safe gate needs no look-ahead. In the terms of supervisory control, 𝖢\mathsf{C} is controllable, and the obligation is the maximally permissive supervisor, which excludes exactly the calls that fail enabledness or preservation at some state in Kn​(v)K_{n}(v) (Ramadge and Wonham, 1987).

Policy engines

A policy engine admits calls by a fixed rule that it decides itself: a decidable gate, whose author must show that it is safe. By Proposition A.1, a safe rule admits only calls whose obligation holds, and if its safety is proved, each call it admits comes with a proof of its obligation: evaluate the rule on the request, and apply the proof of safety. An agent constrained by a safe policy can therefore run under PC2, which admits, in addition, every other call whose obligation is proved: the agent may follow any strategy whose calls keep the contract. A fixed rule rejects safe calls wherever it is stricter than the obligation, as it must be wherever the obligation is undecidable. In the travel contract, a rule that caps each of three nights at 600 EUR keeps the budget of 2000 EUR, and rejects a first night at 900 EUR followed by two at 500 EUR, although these keep the budget too. The exact rule is the obligation itself: a policy engine can enforce it only where it is decidable, and only after someone has derived it from the contract, while PC2 derives it and checks a proof of it.

Appendix B Details on the proof-checking program

Algorithm B.1 gives the routines used by Alg. 1 to check a request while control continues. The check concerns a particular tool, input and recorded view. Its correctness therefore requires both a sound checker, as in A1, and the connection between the checked statement and the call required by .

Forming the obligation. For a request (𝖳,i,k0,n,π)({\mathsf{T}},i,k_{0},n,\pi), the Airlock retrieves the unchanged view v⁡[k0]v[k_{0}] and checks that 𝖳∈𝒯{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T} and i∈I𝖳i\in I_{\mathsf{T}}. It then forms the statement Obl𝖳⩽n​(i,v⁡[k0])\mathrm{Obl}_{\mathsf{T}}^{\leqslant n}(i,v[k_{0}]) from the contract’s agreed definitions. The submitted proof must establish this statement under the permitted axioms. Checking a statement supplied by the requester would not suffice, since it might express a different condition.

This requirement also concerns how a statement is represented. Source text acquires its meaning from the notations and definitions in scope. For example, a macro that replaces the written obligation with True would make trivial a valid proof of the resulting statement, while establishing nothing about the requested call. Agents have exploited changes to notation in a Lean submission system in this way (Paglieri et al., 2026). The issue is the connection between the intended statement and the one checked, a distinction discussed by Pollack (1998); Wiedijk (2012).

In Lean, the obligation can instead be formed directly as an expression in the kernel’s language, using the fixed contract definitions and an encoding of the recorded view. That encoding must faithfully represent the view. A kernel expression does not depend on submitted notation or macros for its meaning. Lean’s export format records such expressions and their dependencies, and comparator checks a submitted solution against an independently supplied statement and permitted axioms (Lean FRO, 2025b; Lean FRO, 2025a). These facilities support the check, provided the statement against which the solution is compared is formed independently of untrusted source.

From a verdict to a call. Each check uses a fixed request and recorded view, and its verdict belongs only to that request. In the pseudocode, 𝗄𝗂𝗅𝗅​_​𝗉𝗋𝗈𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌\mathsf{kill\_process} cancels the previous check before its replacement starts, so the cancelled check cannot subsequently publish a verdict. Replacing a request also discards any earlier verdict. The execution loop checks that the current request remains within its control window before running it, and 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗎𝗆𝖾​_​𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿\mathsf{consume\_proof} prevents its reuse.

The invocation must use the same tool and input that appear in the checked obligation. For an input containing executable code, this also requires the runtime behaviour of that code to agree with the definitions used in the proof, a requirement on the compiler and runtime. Running the checker in a separate process allows control to continue while a proof is checked. The checker must also be prevented from altering the contract, recorded views or execution of a running routine. Process separation supports these requirements, but must be accompanied by the access restrictions needed to satisfy A4 and A7.

Independent checking. The same formal proof can be checked by several implementations. If acceptance requires all of them to accept the same statement under the agreed definitions and axioms, soundness of any one of them suffices for soundness of the combined check, provided their results are combined correctly. Lean provides export-based checking and, from version 4.35, an option to run several bundled checkers (Lean FRO, 2026). This offers a way to reduce reliance on one implementation of the checking rules.

Rocq also has a separately implemented checker through the MetaRocq project. Its safe checker is written and verified in Rocq for PCUIC, a formal calculus underlying Rocq. Its correctness and completeness results concern that calculus under their stated assumptions, including strong normalization (Sozeau et al., 2020; Sozeau et al., 2025). Within this scope it provides another way to support A1.

Using different proof assistants requires an additional connection between their statements. For example, recent work translates MiniF2F statements into Rocq, with human review of their semantic agreement (Viennot et al., 2025). To use such a translation for a PC2 obligation, one also needs a proof of the translated statement and a justification that it expresses the intended obligation. Rechecking the same formal statement with another kernel does not require this translation.

Appendix C A possible design for the control ctrl

The control routine of Sec. 3.5.1 keeps a contract compliant while the agent prepares calls and their proofs are checked. Depending on the state it reads, it waits, corrects the state or closes the contract. We now explain how these choices can establish the certificate required by A3, and illustrate the argument with a compute budget. The construction connects the clause to the interventions available to control: every compliant active state must leave at least one of these choices safe.

Establishing the certificate. Fix the idle period pp and the region CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}} of Sec. 3.5.1. Outside 𝐴𝑐𝑡\mathit{Act}, a compliant state belongs to CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}}, so the model of one idle period admits only compliant states. In 𝐴𝑐𝑡∩𝐹𝑖𝑥\mathit{Act}\cap\mathit{Fix}, the correcting routine must preserve CC throughout its execution and return to CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}}. In 𝐸𝑛𝑑\mathit{End}, the termination routine must preserve CC until the contract closes, including at closing. Each branch must also be enabled wherever it is selected. The model 𝖣ctrl{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}} covers the whole control period, from its initial reading until it is ready to hand over to the next invocation. The branch guarantees must therefore include the outside changes and costs over that whole period. Together, these conditions give the controller line of A3.

Initialization supplies its other role. From 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦\mathit{Ready}, the initializer establishes CC before making the contract active, as when it sets the status to 𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{ongoing} at the end of initialization. From the other inactive states it leaves the contract inactive. Providing an enabled model for both cases gives the initializer requirements of A3. Only the tests used by the routine, namely 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦\mathit{Ready}, 𝐴𝑐𝑡\mathit{Act} and 𝐹𝑖𝑥\mathit{Fix}, need to be decidable. The clause and CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}} can remain more general predicates, with their relationship to these tests established by the certificate.

This construction includes the simpler controllers discussed in Sec. 3.5.1. If outside changes preserve CC, then Cidle=CC_{\mathrm{idle}}=C and control can simply wait, as in the stability condition of rely–guarantee reasoning (Jones, 1983). If no correction is supplied, control waits or terminates, as in the travel contract. When correction is available, returning well inside CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}} leaves room for further activity before another intervention is needed.

When a control invocation from a compliant active state returns without closing the contract, the state is either in CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}} after correction or in a state reached by one idle period from that region. This describes the states at the completion of control, as illustrated in Fig. 4(a). A requested tool may subsequently move the state elsewhere within CC. The delayed obligations in panel (b) use the full model 𝖣ctrl{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}}, which must also include the intermediate states of control invocations.

Example: a compute budget. A company lets an agent run cloud jobs within a budget BB, with the contract to close by a deadline dd. The state records the bill bb, an upper bound rr on the combined charging rate of the running jobs, the time tt and the contract’s status ℓ\ell. Outside changes can increase the bill at rate at most rr or stop jobs, but only an authorized call can add jobs or increase the rate. In this example we model readings and branch selection as instantaneous, while stopping the jobs can take up to δ\delta units of time. The contract must reserve enough money and time for this shutdown.

To express that reserve throughout execution, the state also records a remaining shutdown allowance hh. While jobs run normally, h=δh=\delta. Once shutdown begins, hh counts down with elapsed time, and the model requires the jobs to have stopped by the time it reaches zero. If no jobs remain, r=h=0r=h=0. We use the clause

𝖢(s):⇔b+rh≤B∧(ℓ=𝗈𝗇𝗀𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗀⟹t+h≤d).\mathsf{C}(s)\quad:\iff\quad b+rh\leq B\quad\wedge\quad\bigl(\ell=\mathsf{ongoing}\ \implies\ t+h\leq d\bigr).

The term r​hrh reserves the maximum further charge during shutdown. Thus the clause protects the budget while retaining the means to stop, and the agent’s calls cannot spend that reserve.

Control can idle for pp whenever

b+r⁡(p+h)≤B,t+p+h≤d.b+r(p+h)\leq B,\qquad t+p+h\leq d.

These decidable tests certify membership in CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}}: throughout the idle period the bill can rise by at most r​prp, while enough money and time remain for shutdown. Use the complement of this tested region for 𝐴𝑐𝑡\mathit{Act}. When only the budget test fails, there is still time to correct the state. A simple fix stops the running jobs and leaves the contract active. When the time test fails, control stops the jobs and closes the contract instead.

Both interventions preserve the clause. After 0≤u≤h0\leq u\leq h time units during shutdown, its model gives b′≤b+r​ub^{\prime}\leq b+ru, r′≤rr^{\prime}\leq r, h′≤h−uh^{\prime}\leq h-u and t′=t+ut^{\prime}=t+u, hence

b′+r′​h′≤b+r​u+r⁡(h−u)=b+r​h≤B,t′+h′≤t+h≤d.b^{\prime}+r^{\prime}h^{\prime}\leq b+ru+r(h-u)=b+rh\leq B,\qquad t^{\prime}+h^{\prime}\leq t+h\leq d.

At completion, r′=h′=0r^{\prime}=h^{\prime}=0. In the correcting branch, the time test held before the intervention, so t′+p≤t+h+p≤dt^{\prime}+p\leq t+h+p\leq d. The resulting state therefore belongs to CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}}. In the terminating branch, shutdown finishes within the reserved time and the contract closes by dd, with the bill still at most BB. Initialization starts the contract only when the waiting tests have been established; otherwise it leaves it inactive.

The same accounting applies to a tool that launches more jobs: its obligation requires the clause, including the shutdown reserve, throughout the call. The call need not leave enough room to wait for another whole period, because control can intervene immediately afterwards. This distinguishes the protection supplied by the contract from the additional room for uninterrupted work supplied by CidleC_{\mathrm{idle}}.

Appendix D Time between operations

takes the operations of the Airlock to be contiguous: each starts when the previous one ends. In an implementation, a routine may return before the host is ready to invoke the next one, and the system can continue to change during this interval. We account for a gap of at most t0t_{0} by including it in the preceding operation and enlarging the tool models accordingly. Together with the sampling convention specified below, this lets us apply the results of Sec. 4 to the extended operations. Their models and control certificate must cover the added intervals.

Extended operations. Between the return of a routine and the invocation of the next one, no tool routine runs. The state can still change, by outside changes: time advances, prices move, mail arrives. Over a time of at most t0t_{0}, these are the changes that the model of 𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾\mathsf{idle} admits (Sec. 3): 𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾​(t0,z,s′′){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}}(t_{0},z,s^{\prime\prime}) holds when outside changes can lead from zz to s′′s^{\prime\prime} within a time of at most t0t_{0}. In particular, 𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾​(t0,z,z){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}}(t_{0},z,z) holds for every zz, since that time may be zero.

For each tool 𝖳∈𝒯∪{ctrl}{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{\texttt{ctrl}\}, let 𝖳′{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime} be the corresponding extended tool, with the same input space. An operation of 𝖳′{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime} executes the routine exec𝖳\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}} and includes the subsequent gap. Its model is

𝖣𝖳′​(i,s,s′′):⇔∃z.𝖣𝖳​(i,s,z)∧𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾​(t0,z,s′′).{\mathsf{D}}_{{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime}}(i,s,s^{\prime\prime})\;:\iff\;\exists z.\ {\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,z)\wedge{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}}(t_{0},z,s^{\prime\prime}). (D.1)

The model of 𝖳′{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime} admits every state that the model of 𝖳{\mathsf{T}} admits, taking z=s′′z=s^{\prime\prime}, and every state that outside changes can reach within t0t_{0} from such a state, in particular from the state in which the routine returns. It is enabled exactly where the model of 𝖳{\mathsf{T}} is. Let 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime} be the contract 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} with the tools 𝖳′{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime}, for 𝖳∈𝒯{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}, and the control tool ctrl′\texttt{ctrl}^{\prime}. Its state space, clauses, view and inactivity test are those of 𝒦{\mathcal{K}}.

An operation of 𝖳′{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime} starts when the Airlock invokes exec𝖳\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}, as an operation of 𝖳{\mathsf{T}} does, but it ends only when the Airlock invokes the next routine, or when the contract closes. It consists of the execution of the routine followed by the time between operations. The underlying tool routine is unchanged, but its extended operation includes the time spent by the host before the next invocation. If the routines run on the intervals [τ1,τ1′],[τ2,τ2′],…[\tau_{1},\tau^{\prime}_{1}],[\tau_{2},\tau^{\prime}_{2}],\dots, with τk′≤τk+1≤τk′+t0\tau^{\prime}_{k}\leq\tau_{k+1}\leq\tau^{\prime}_{k}+t_{0}, the operations of 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} are these intervals, while those of 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime} are [τ1,τ2],[τ2,τ3],…[\tau_{1},\tau_{2}],[\tau_{2},\tau_{3}],\dots. The extended operations are therefore contiguous, as required by .

Readings at operation boundaries. To use Lemma 1, a recorded view must describe the state at a boundary between the operations counted by its window. We therefore use the following sampling convention for the extended operations: the reading associated with a completed operation is taken at the handoff to the next routine, and views and the inactivity test use that reading. Sampling and dispatch are treated as a single boundary event in this abstraction. This convention, together with the bound t0t_{0}, is a condition of the construction. It connects the readings to the extended operations as required by . Together with the exclusion of intervening requested calls in , this ensures that a call based on an earlier recorded view is separated from its reading only by complete operations of ctrl′\texttt{ctrl}^{\prime}, so the control-window argument applies.

Guarantees for the extended operations. With this sampling convention, we apply the definitions and results of Sec. 3 and 4 to 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime}. In A2, E𝖳′E_{{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime}} now describes the states reached throughout the extended operation, including the gap. The Airlock forms the obligations of 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime} from the models 𝖣𝖳′{\mathsf{D}}_{{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime}}, and their windows from 𝖣ctrl′{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}^{\prime}}. Under A1, A2, A3 and A4 for 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime}, Thm. 1 gives the clauses at every instant from the start, including the time between operations, which now lies within operations of 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime}. Since (𝖳|𝖯𝗋𝖾)′=𝖳′|𝖯𝗋𝖾({\mathsf{T}}|_{\mathsf{Pre}})^{\prime}={\mathsf{T}}^{\prime}|_{\mathsf{Pre}}, the settlement tool of a standard contract remains goal-gated, and since outside changes do not modify the label, Thm. 2 applies too. For t0=0t_{0}=0, 𝖣𝗂𝖽𝗅𝖾​(0,⋅,⋅){\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{idle}}(0,\cdot,\cdot) is the identity, and 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime} is 𝒦{\mathcal{K}}.

These guarantees require the assumptions to hold for 𝒦′{\mathcal{K}}^{\prime}. Coverage must account for the routine and the following gap, and the control certificate must establish initialization and compliance for the enlarged model 𝖣ctrl′{\mathsf{D}}_{\texttt{ctrl}^{\prime}}. For an idling branch of duration pp, this requires accounting for up to p+t0p+t_{0} of outside changes. The correcting and terminating routines must be checked against their enlarged models as well. The agent’s obligations also use the enlarged models, so an accepted proof establishes compliance during the call and its following gap.

To apply the world-safety result of Thm. 3, E^𝖳′\widehat{E}_{{\mathsf{T}}^{\prime}} must likewise describe the world and state throughout the extended operation, and A5 must hold over that whole interval. Preserving the correspondence during the added gap then connects the compliance guarantee to safety in the world through A6.

Appendix E Two worked examples of correspondence

This appendix works through two correspondences of the kind studied in Sec. 5.1. In the payment ledger, the state bounds what happens in the world, as safety requires. In the booking confirmations, what the state records must be true of the world, as completion requires.

E.1  A payment ledger

The structure needed is simple, and we describe it in words. The contract lets the agent pay merchants within a budget BB, fees included, through a payment provider that issues payment instructions with a spending limit, such as single-use virtual cards, pre-authorizations, or payment mandates with a maximum amount (Google, 2025).

  • •

    The state contains a ledger kept by the Airlock: a list of entries, each with three fields, an identifier, a payee and a limit.

  • •

    The world contains the provider’s records for the account: for each instruction it has issued, its identifier, payee and limit, and the charges posted against it.

  • •

    The tool 𝗉𝖺𝗒⁡(m,q)\mathsf{pay}(m,q) pays the merchant mm up to qq. Its routine appends the entry (j,m,q)(j,m,q) to the ledger, under a fresh identifier jj, and only then asks the provider to issue the instruction (j,m,q)(j,m,q). A retry reuses jj, which the provider treats as an idempotency key. The model of 𝗉𝖺𝗒\mathsf{pay} admits the ledger unchanged or with the new entry.

For an identifier jj, write rj​(s)r_{j}(s) for the limit of its entry in the ledger, uj​(w)u_{j}(w) for the limit the provider has issued under jj, and aj​(w)a_{j}(w) for the total charged under jj, each zero if there is no such entry, instruction or charge. The clause bounds what the ledger has reserved, and safety bounds what has actually been charged:

b⁡(s):=∑jrj​(s),a⁡(w):=∑jaj​(w),𝖢⁡(s):=b⁡(s)≤B,𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w):=a⁡(w)≤B.b(s):=\sum_{j}r_{j}(s),\qquad a(w):=\sum_{j}a_{j}(w),\qquad\mathsf{C}(s):=b(s)\leq B,\qquad\mathsf{Safe}(w):=a(w)\leq B. (E.1)

The budget bound remains part of the clause at closing, so settlement or termination cannot discharge the obligation to respect it. With this model, admissibility of 𝗉𝖺𝗒⁡(m,q)\mathsf{pay}(m,q) at a compliant state reduces to b⁡(s)+q≤Bb(s)+q\leq B, as for the tools of Sec. 3.5.2. When the view reveals the reserved total, the ordinary obligation reduces to the same inequality. In the travel contract, b⁡(s)b(s) is the amount 𝑠𝑝𝑒𝑛𝑡\mathit{spent} in Sec. 2.2: it counts reservations, not receipts. The correspondence relates the provider’s records to the ledger:

ρ(w,s)⇔∀j.aj(w)≤uj(w)≤rj(s).\rho(w,s)\quad\iff\quad\forall j.\quad a_{j}(w)\leq u_{j}(w)\leq r_{j}(s). (E.2)

Every issued limit is covered by an entry of the ledger, and every charge stays within its limit.

Two conditions maintain this correspondence. The reservation discipline: only the Airlock’s routines ask the provider to issue instructions, each after recording its entry; entries are never removed or lowered, issued limits never change, and retries reuse their identifier. The service condition: the provider lets the charges under an instruction, fees and retries included, reach at most its limit, and accepts no charge without an instruction. Both conditions apply at every instant, to all routines and outside interactions. Charges may arrive after a routine returns, so entries are retained to cover them.

Proposition E.1 (Preserving budget correspondence).

The reservation discipline and service condition preserve E.2 whenever it holds initially. In particular, they imply the first line of A5.

Proof.

For an existing instruction, uj≤rju_{j}\leq r_{j} persists because its issued limit is fixed and its reservation never decreases. A new instruction satisfies the inequality because reservation precedes issuance. Before issuance, uj=0≤rju_{j}=0\leq r_{j}. The service condition gives aj≤uja_{j}\leq u_{j} at every instant, so correspondence holds throughout, including between routines. ∎

Summing E.2 gives a⁡(w)≤b⁡(s)a(w)\leq b(s), so the clause implies 𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w)\mathsf{Safe}(w), establishing the safety implication of A6. A new entry with limit qq requires b⁡(s)+q≤Bb(s)+q\leq B at every invocation state admitted by the view and control window. Under A1, A2, A3 and A4, Thm. 1 preserves this budget clause. Together with Proposition E.1, and a start in which the empty ledger describes the account, as for a fresh account with no issued instructions or charges (A5), this yields the world-safety guarantee. Recording expenditure only when a receipt arrives would instead leave issued instructions temporarily uncovered. The ledger reserves a quantity before it can be consumed, as the escrow method of transaction processing does for bounded quantities (O’Neil, 1986), and records an action before performing it, as write-ahead logging does (Mohan et al., 1992).

The reservation discipline concerns the routine, which can be verified, and the custody of the provider’s credentials, which only the Airlock may use (Sec. 6.1). The service condition concerns the provider: it is a property of a service that the parties do not build, which the provider must support or the parties must accept. Where a provider allows charges to exceed a limit by a tolerance, the routine must record the limit plus that tolerance.

The guarantee can extend beyond closing. Suppose the hypotheses of Thm. 3 hold and the session closes at time τc\tau_{c} with state scs_{c}. If no new instructions can be issued afterwards, existing issued limits remain fixed, and the service condition continues to hold, then for every τ≥τc\tau\geq\tau_{c},

a⁡(w⁡(τ))≤b⁡(sc)≤B.a(w(\tau))\leq b(s_{c})\leq B. (E.3)

The reservations at closing already cover the charges that may still arrive. This protection therefore survives without the Airlock continuing to run, provided the restrictions on issuance and charging remain effective.

E.2  Booking confirmations

The ledger construction controls which instructions can produce charges. A booking confirmation raises a different question: what does a service’s response establish, and for how long?

Example 3 (Booking confirmations).

Let R⁡(s)R(s) be a finite set of recorded confirmations (b,d)(b,d), where bb identifies a particular reservation and dd is its expiry time. Write 𝖨𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾𝖽⁡(w,b,d)\mathsf{Issued}(w,b,d) when the world’s history contains the agreed service’s confirmation of this reservation until dd, and 𝖧𝖾𝗅𝖽⁡(w,b)\mathsf{Held}(w,b) when the hotel actually holds it. With t𝒲​(w)t_{\mathcal{W}}(w) denoting time in the world, consider

ρ𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗄(w,s)⇔∀(b,d)∈R(s).𝖨𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾𝖽(w,b,d)∧(t𝒲(w)<d⟹𝖧𝖾𝗅𝖽(w,b)).\rho_{\mathsf{book}}(w,s)\quad\iff\quad\forall(b,d)\in R(s).\quad\mathsf{Issued}(w,b,d)\ \land\ \bigl(t_{\mathcal{W}}(w)<d\implies\mathsf{Held}(w,b)\bigr). (E.4)

The first conjunct states what the service reported. The second connects that report to a reservation still held before expiry. After expiry, the record continues to describe a past confirmation, but no longer asserts that the reservation is held.

The recording condition requires entries to be added only from authenticated confirmations of the agreed service, with the reservation and expiry recorded correctly. Existing entries may be retained or removed, and any replacement must meet the same condition. The reservation condition requires every confirmed reservation to be held until its stated expiry, including during other operations and between routines. This condition concerns both the service issuing the confirmation and the hotel holding the reservation. A confirmation with an expiry is a lease: a grant that holds until a stated time (Gray and Cheriton, 1989).

Proposition E.2 (Preserving booking correspondence).

The recording and reservation conditions in Example 3 preserve E.4 whenever it holds initially, provided the world’s history retains issued confirmations. They therefore establish the booking component of the first line of A5.

Proof.

Consider any later instant and an entry (b,d)(b,d) still in the record. It was present initially or added from a correctly recorded confirmation. In either case, 𝖨𝗌𝗌𝗎𝖾𝖽⁡(w,b,d)\mathsf{Issued}(w,b,d) holds, since history retains that event. If t𝒲​(w)<dt_{\mathcal{W}}(w)<d, the reservation condition gives 𝖧𝖾𝗅𝖽⁡(w,b)\mathsf{Held}(w,b). Both conjuncts therefore hold throughout execution, including between routines. ∎

Authentication supports the recording condition, but does not establish the reservation condition. It establishes where a report came from, not that the report is true, a distinction familiar from authenticated data feeds and blockchain oracles (Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020; Eskandari et al., 2021). The service may have sent an authentic confirmation even though the hotel later cancels the booking. Conversely, the reservation condition need not prevent cancellation after expiry. For a goal that requires the reservation still to be held, the contract must also establish that the confirmation has not expired when settlement begins. For instance, a further correspondence claim t𝒲​(w)≤t​(s)t_{\mathcal{W}}(w)\leq t(s), where t⁡(s)t(s) is a conservative time bound, makes t⁡(s)<dt(s)<d sufficient. This bound must cover delays before invocation: an earlier clock reading alone does not provide it. Together with E.4, it supplies the connection from a recorded confirmation to 𝖧𝖾𝗅𝖽\mathsf{Held} needed by Cor. 4.

For the travel contract, this gives the following goal in the world.

Example 4 (Settlement of a travel contract).

For the travel contract, let 𝑁𝑖𝑔ℎ𝑡𝑠\mathit{Nights} be the requested nights, and let 𝖱𝗈𝗈𝗆𝖧𝖾𝗅𝖽⁡(w,n)\mathsf{RoomHeld}(w,n) mean that a hotel holds a reservation for the traveller on night nn. A possible world goal is

𝐺𝑜𝑎𝑙𝒲(w):=(∀n∈𝑁𝑖𝑔ℎ𝑡𝑠.𝖱𝗈𝗈𝗆𝖧𝖾𝗅𝖽(w,n))∧𝖵𝗂𝗌𝖺𝖦𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗍𝖾𝖽(w),\mathit{Goal}_{\mathcal{W}}(w):=\bigl(\forall n\in\mathit{Nights}.\ \mathsf{RoomHeld}(w,n)\bigr)\land\mathsf{VisaGranted}(w), (E.5)

where the second conjunct means that the traveller’s visa has been granted. Under its hypotheses, Cor. 4 ensures that these conditions hold when settlement begins. A goal expressed through recorded confirmations supports this conclusion only if correspondence connects those records to reservations still valid at that instant.

Appendix F What goes wrong without isolation

The examples of Appendix E show that relating the contract’s state to the world requires conditions on the routines and on the services they use. In the payment example, the argument relies on every issued instruction being backed by a ledger entry and on the provider respecting its spending limit. To apply that argument to a system used by an agent, we must also consider the access that the agent has to the account and the ledger. If it can issue a payment directly or erase an entry, the fact that the Airlock’s payment routine follows the prescribed procedure is no longer sufficient.

We are interested in systems where this access can be restricted by design. For instance, keeping the payment credentials and ledger under the Airlock’s control can ensure that instructions are issued only by its routines. The tool model 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} can then describe the state changes caused by these operations without also including arbitrary modifications of the ledger by the agent. The obligation for a proposed payment checks whether the modeled changes respect the budget, while the provider’s spending limits connect the recorded amounts to actual charges. Section 6.1 develops capability modules, which combine access to a resource with guarantees about the operations performed on it. This appendix examines why protecting this access matters, by following what an action outside the proof gate does to the assumptions of Thm. 3, as illustrated in Fig. 5.

Ungated interactions. Consider an agent that can invoke a routine in two ways. It can submit a request to the Airlock, which checks the corresponding obligation before executing the call, or invoke the routine directly without providing a proof. We call the second form of access ungated. To see how it can affect the guarantees, suppose that an invocation authorized by the Airlock starts from a compliant active state ss with ρ⁡(w,s)\rho(w,s). While it runs, an ungated action makes the world unsafe, so that ¬𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w′)\neg\mathsf{Safe}(w^{\prime}). The running invocation may be control, as in Fig. 5, or a requested tool. In either case, E^𝖳\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}} includes this change, since it describes everything that can happen to the world and state during the invocation.

If the state remains unchanged, it still satisfies 𝖢⁡(s)\mathsf{C}(s). Under A6, it can therefore no longer describe the unsafe world:

𝖢⁡(s)∧¬𝖲𝖺𝖿𝖾⁡(w′)⟹¬ρ⁡(w′,s).\mathsf{C}(s)\land\neg\mathsf{Safe}(w^{\prime})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\neg\rho(w^{\prime},s). (F.1)

This violates fidelity, A5, because correspondence held at the start of the enabled invocation and has been lost while it runs. Detecting the change afterwards cannot restore a guarantee that was required to hold at every instant.

If instead the state changes to s′s^{\prime} and ρ⁡(w′,s′)\rho(w^{\prime},s^{\prime}) holds, adequacy requires ¬𝖢⁡(s′)\neg\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}). The question is then whether the tool model 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} includes this state. Omitting it violates coverage, A2, since it is a possible effect of the running invocation. Including it means that the invocation is not admissible from ss. For control this contradicts A3, and for a requested tool it contradicts the admissibility established from its accepted obligation under the assumptions of Thm. 1. Finally, if we allow ρ⁡(w′,s′)\rho(w^{\prime},s^{\prime}) to hold while keeping 𝖢⁡(s′)\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}) true, the unsafe world is described by a compliant state and adequacy itself fails. The three branches of Fig. 5 illustrate these different ways in which an ungated action can invalidate the assumptions.

Restricting effects. We could try to account for ungated access by enlarging 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} to cover all the state changes it makes possible. Suppose, however, that these changes include some s′s^{\prime} with E𝖳​(i,s,s′)E_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}) and ¬𝖢⁡(s′)\neg\mathsf{C}(s^{\prime}). For any model that includes this outcome, 𝒜𝖳​(i,s)\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s) is false, because admissibility requires every state described by the model to satisfy 𝖢\mathsf{C}. If this happens for every requested call throughout execution, the proof gate rejects all of them. Provided control remains admissible as required by A3 and the other hypotheses of Thm. 3 hold, the system still remains safe. It can continue running control, but cannot execute any requested action to carry out the task. Thus covering all possible behaviour can preserve the safety guarantee while making the system unusable for its intended purpose.

A separate difficulty arises when the ungated action changes the world without changing the state. Such an action appears in E^𝖳\widehat{E}_{\mathsf{T}}, even if it introduces no additional state into E𝖳E_{\mathsf{T}}. As F.1 shows, a compliant state cannot remain a faithful description of an unsafe world under adequacy. Enlarging 𝖣𝖳{\mathsf{D}}_{\mathsf{T}} cannot resolve this failure of fidelity. This is why we consider restrictions on the agent’s actual access, alongside conditions on the models used by the checker. Section 5.2 states the corresponding restriction as A7.

Appendix G A formal account of isolation

Lemma 2 allows coverage and fidelity established for reference executions to apply when an agent is present. The reason is that, during an invocation, the agent cannot change the protected system or introduce new possibilities for its evolution. This appendix gives a stepwise formulation of that argument. It uses the method of proving non-interference through conditions on individual steps (Goguen and Meseguer, 1984; Rushby, 1992).

We fix 𝖳∈𝒯∪{ctrl}{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{\texttt{ctrl}\}, an input ii and an invocation of its routine R=exec𝖳​(i)R=\texttt{exec}_{\mathsf{T}}(i). The routine runs alongside the environment, the host and the agent. The environment includes external services and the passage of time. The host includes the Airlock’s loop and checker. As in Sec. 5.2, reference executions suppress the agent’s steps while leaving the other processes present.

Definition G.1 (Configurations and invocation prefixes).

A configuration is a tuple c=(w,s,r,u,a)c=(w,s,r,u,a), where w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, s∈Σs\in\Sigma, and rr, uu and aa are the local states of the routine, host and agent, respectively. The routine state rr contains its fixed input and records whether it has returned. For each actor b∈{R,𝖾𝗇𝗏,𝗁𝗈𝗌𝗍,𝖺𝗀}b\in\{R,\mathsf{env},\mathsf{host},\mathsf{ag}\}, let →b\to_{b} be its step relation on configurations. An invocation prefix is a finite sequence c0→b1c1⋯→bmcmc_{0}\to_{b_{1}}c_{1}\cdots\to_{b_{m}}c_{m} starting with the routine in its initial state on ii, in which the routine has not returned at any cjc_{j} with j<mj<m. The protected part of a configuration is

κR​(w,s,r,u,a):=(w,s,r).\kappa_{R}(w,s,r,u,a):=(w,s,r).

A reference prefix is an invocation prefix containing no step of 𝖺𝗀\mathsf{ag}. Write c↝dc\rightsquigarrow d for a finite sequence, possibly empty, of steps of RR, 𝖾𝗇𝗏\mathsf{env} and 𝗁𝗈𝗌𝗍\mathsf{host} from cc to dd within the same invocation, with no step after the routine has returned.

A prefix may end before the routine returns, or at its return. This is necessary because the effect relations describe every state reached during execution. When the step model represents the executions of Sec. 5.1, each world–state pair reached at any instant must be represented by a finite invocation prefix. In particular, a step that advances time must allow prefixes ending at intermediate instants if the world or state changes during that step. Sampling only the entry and return of a routine would not describe the effects used in the main results.

For an agent α\alpha, whose processes determine →𝖺𝗀\to_{\mathsf{ag}}, let E^𝖳α​(i,w,s,w′,s′)\widehat{E}^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}) hold when an invocation prefix starting with world ww and state ss ends with world w′w^{\prime} and state s′s^{\prime}. Define E^𝖳∙\widehat{E}^{\bullet}_{\mathsf{T}} in the same way using reference prefixes. The state effects are their projections, as in 14. The initial configurations and the step relations of the other actors are the same in both cases.

Conditions on steps. The following conditions give a sufficient stepwise formulation of isolation for this model. They are required for each tool and input, for configurations of the same invocation and steps taken before the routine returns.

  1. (NI1)

    Preservation by the agent. If c→𝖺𝗀c′c\to_{\mathsf{ag}}c^{\prime}, then κR​(c′)=κR​(c)\kappa_{R}(c^{\prime})=\kappa_{R}(c).

  2. (NI2)

    Independence of the protected evolution. If c→bc′c\to_{b}c^{\prime} with b≠𝖺𝗀b\neq\mathsf{ag} and κR​(d)=κR​(c)\kappa_{R}(d)=\kappa_{R}(c), then there is a configuration d′d^{\prime} such that d↝d′d\rightsquigarrow d^{\prime} and κR​(d′)=κR​(c′)\kappa_{R}(d^{\prime})=\kappa_{R}(c^{\prime}).

(NI1) expresses the restriction on the agent’s access in A7: its computation and submission of requests leave the running routine, world and state unchanged. (NI2) expresses the independence needed to remove that computation. When two configurations agree on the protected quantities, a change produced by the other actors from one must also be possible from the other without an agent step. The matching sequence may be empty when the original step leaves the protected quantities unchanged. Thus, for example, a checker’s private progress need not be reproduced step for step.

These conditions must be established for the interfaces and execution environment that enforce isolation. They do not require knowing how the agent chooses its requests or proofs. Host and service actions remain in reference executions, and their effects must still be covered by the tool models. Execution integrity, A4, continues to govern the scheduling of invocations and the connection between requests, views and calls.

Lemma G.1 (Isolation, stepwise formulation).

For any agent α\alpha satisfying (NI1) and (NI2), every invocation prefix has a reference prefix starting from the same configuration and ending in a configuration with the same protected part. Consequently, for all inputs, worlds and states,

E^𝖳α​(i,w,s,w′,s′)⟹E^𝖳∙​(i,w,s,w′,s′),E𝖳α​(i,s,s′)⟹E𝖳∙​(i,s,s′).\widehat{E}^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime})\implies\widehat{E}^{\bullet}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,w,s,w^{\prime},s^{\prime}),\qquad E^{\alpha}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime})\implies E^{\bullet}_{\mathsf{T}}(i,s,s^{\prime}).
Proof.

Consider an invocation prefix c0→b1c1⋯→bmcmc_{0}\to_{b_{1}}c_{1}\cdots\to_{b_{m}}c_{m}. We construct a reference prefix starting at c0c_{0} whose endpoint djd_{j} satisfies κR​(dj)=κR​(cj)\kappa_{R}(d_{j})=\kappa_{R}(c_{j}), by induction on jj.

For j=0j=0, the empty prefix suffices. Suppose the prefix has been constructed up to j<mj<m. If bj+1=𝖺𝗀b_{j+1}=\mathsf{ag}, (NI1) gives κR​(cj+1)=κR​(cj)\kappa_{R}(c_{j+1})=\kappa_{R}(c_{j}), so the same reference prefix serves, with dj+1=djd_{j+1}=d_{j}. Otherwise, (NI2) gives a sequence dj↝dj+1d_{j}\rightsquigarrow d_{j+1} with κR​(dj+1)=κR​(cj+1)\kappa_{R}(d_{j+1})=\kappa_{R}(c_{j+1}), which we append. Since j<mj<m, the routine has not returned at cjc_{j} or at its matching configuration djd_{j}. The appended sequence takes no step after return, so the concatenation is a reference prefix.

At j=mj=m, the constructed prefix starts at the same invocation and has the same final world and state. It therefore witnesses the implication for E^\widehat{E}. Projection on states gives the implication for EE. ∎

Thus coverage and both parts of fidelity for reference executions also hold for actual executions, as required by Lemma 2.
